title: KAIST aims to extend the lifespan of anode-free batteries
content: Researchers at the South Korean Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) have developed an approach to extend the lifespan of anode-free lithium-metal batteries. They are leveraging a manufacturing process from the semiconductor industry and a coating just ten nanometers thick.

title: Denver man traps Waymo robotaxis with cones, eggs them at least 30 times
content:
autonomous driving
Fred Lambert
| Nov 26 2026 - 6:36 am PT
The next-generation Waymo Ojai, built by Zeekr. Source: Waymo
A man in Denver has found a cheap way to beat Waymo’s self-driving system: a few orange traffic cones and a carton of eggs.
Waymo says it has counted at least 30 egg attacks on its robotaxis in Denver, all believed to be the same man. And the Denver District Attorney’s Office has declined to file charges, calling it a civil matter, according to
The New York Times
Box it in, then egg it
The method is laid out in a Denver police report filed last month. The man pulls up in front of a Waymo somewhere in or around downtown, takes orange cones out of his trunk, and sets them around the robotaxi so it can’t drive off. Then come the eggs, sometimes thrown from his driver’s seat, sometimes after he gets out.
He leaves in a silver Toyota Corolla. Per the report, that car belongs to a fleet leased out to Lyft drivers. The man hasn’t been identified, and Lyft didn’t comment.
A Waymo investigator took seven of the incidents to police. Each egged vehicle had to come out of service for cleaning, and the detailing bill came to about $2,000. No permanent damage.
Police brought their findings to prosecutors, who decided “no criminal charges” were appropriate. A spokesperson for the DA told the Times the office is now collecting evidence on potential damage and will work with the city attorney to find “the most appropriate legal mechanism to make this behavior stop.”
At least one Waymo had a rider inside. Jeff Hunley was headed to the Union Station neighborhood in September when his robotaxi got hit. He filmed it, said he felt safe in the car, and got his fare refunded.
Two months into Denver
opened its Denver service to the public on September 1
, alongside San Diego and Tampa. The company now runs more than 100 vehicles across 60 square miles of the city, and Mayor Mike Johnston is a fan. He called them popular and affordable, and couldn’t resist adding that “overall they’re a good egg.”
The rest of November hasn’t been as friendly. California’s DMV ordered Waymo’s driverless vehicles off state freeways on November 11 after robotaxis drove into active construction zones and one tried to get past a CHP traffic break. Waymo responded by pausing freeway rides in every US market.
And vandalism isn’t new for Waymo. We covered it when
at least five of its I-Pace robotaxis were set on fire during protests in Los Angeles
last year.
Why the cones work
Putting a single cone on a Waymo’s hood to freeze it has been a known trick since San Francisco activists did it in 2023. Ringing the car with cones works for the same reason: the Waymo Driver is built to respect them, and it won’t push through.
A human driver getting pelted with eggs would just roll over a cone and leave. A robotaxi sits there and takes it.
That’s the correct default. You don’t want a driverless car deciding when a cone is optional, especially two weeks after regulators pulled Waymo off California freeways for ignoring work zones. But it means anyone with a trunk full of cones can pin a robotaxi in place for as long as they want.
Electrek’s Take
We’ll try to keep the egg puns to a minimum. Mostly.
This is small-time vandalism. Two grand in cleaning, no injuries, no lasting damage. But it shows a real weakness in robotaxis: they’re designed to be the most cautious car on the road, and a determined person can turn that caution against them in under a minute. The car can’t escape, can’t honk its way out, and apparently can’t stop the same guy from coming back 30 times.
The DA’s call is hard to follow. Prosecutors have a repeat pattern, a vehicle tied to a known fleet operator, rider video, and robotaxis that are basically rolling camera rigs. And still no charges. If someone boxed in a regular taxi with a passenger inside and started throwing things at it, we suspect the answer would be different.
At the same time, I can’t help but respect the guy’s dedication.

title: These are the e-bike sales you should really care about this Black Friday
content:
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Nov 26 2026 - 5:31 am PT
It’s that time of year again; Black Friday approaches! And while the e-bike sales have been pretty good all month, there’s no better day than today to find an amazing deal on a new way around your city (or a fitness e-bike, leisure e-bike, cargo e-bike, etc…)!
A lot of sites will throw a lot of affiliate links at you today for anything they can hawk for a few bucks (this site included from our deals team, probably). But this isn’t that. I’m a professional e-bike rider and tester, and the deals below are only for bikes I actually ride, and for companies I would actually recommend to my own family and friends. Basically, this is the good stuff.
Lectric eBikes
Let’s start with Lectric eBikes, since, as the largest e-bike company in North America, they have long been setting the standard for incredible deals and value in the e-bike industry. I’ve long said that you can’t get better value than here. Sure, you can find lower-priced e-bikes out there, but not at this quality level and with this level of customer support.
Lectric’s sales are usually defined by huge collections of free accessories added to their already low-priced e-bikes, further increasing the value. But this year there are also some legit price drops as well. See all of their
Black Friday Sales packages here.
The major standouts for me have always been the XP and XP Lite lines.
The latest of each, the
XP Lite3
, offer bundle deals with savings of up to
, respectively. For price drops, you’ll find that both the
Lectrix XPLite 2
XPTrike2
are marked down to new record-low prices.
I’m also a huge fan of their cargo bike, the
Lectric XPedition2
, which has savings of up to
thanks to those impressive bundles.
But you should also explore the
rest of their deals
because just about everything is either marked down or comes with a crazy amount of free accessories that you can’t get for this price any other time of the year!
Ride1Up is another major value leader in the space, and in fact, I’ve been using the Ride1Up Roadster V3 as my everyday commuter e-bike since the summer.
I’m set to surpass 1,000 miles on it (1,600 km) by the end of the month!
That bike is marked down $100 to
just $1,295
right now, making it a major deal for a lightweight, 40 lb (18 kg) commuter e-bike that doubles as a gravel bike. Ask me
how I know
that it can handle hard off-roading, too!
You can also save $150 on
the Vorsa
, which is an awesome all-around e-bike with multiple levels for riders who want higher or lower performance.
The new Portola 02 folder is a killer deal at $100 off
for just $795
(that’s a crazy price!). If you want to go big and powerful, the
will crush Super73 and is doing so
for $500 off
Last but not least, the Prodigy V2 Eco is
just $1,295
after the $100 deal, which is literally the most affordable Bosch-powered electric bike in the world. The only thing stopping me from buying that bike is that I already have one, though at this price, part of me wonders if I should get a spare for friends to use!
Basically, Ride1Up has a ton of
Black Friday Sales
going on now, and you can check them all out
Monarc Bikes
If you want to go a bit further up the quality ladder to get a more premium e-bike, but you still don’t want to spend $2k+, then you should
check out Monarc Bikes
. It was founded by Lectric eBikes as an offshoot that could focus on building higher-end models while still leveraging Lectric’s industry heavyweight status to get better pricing. That means the company can offer higher-end e-bikes that rival some of the bike shop brands, while still offering direct-to-consumer pricing, 5-year warranties, and industry-leading local customer support by phone and email.
The two models they’ve launched so far are the urban-focused Tracer and the off-road-optimized Marker, though you better believe they’ve got more interesting stuff coming, likely next year. For now, though, these two models cover most folks’ needs and come with higher-end parts like quad-piston hydraulic disc brakes, reverse arch forks, Bafang’s powerful motors, large batteries, and impressive add-ons like rear-facing radar to keep tabs on approaching cars.
The company started by selling e-bikes that came with a free spare battery, but has recently opened up options for single or even no-battery bikes, meaning if you previously bought a Monarc model and already have that free spare battery, you can save a bunch of money by buying only the bike and using your spare battery across the line. Yep, it’s like the power drill model!
You can see all of the
sales and deals here!
JackRabbit
JackRabbit
may be a bit of a divisive brand due to how different the bikes look, but I freakin’ love these things! My JackRabbit OG is one of my prized possessions, and I just love how much performance and convenience JackRabbit has been able to pack into small-format two-wheelers that start at barely 25 lb (11 kg).
Literally every one of their micro e-bikes is 20% off, meaning you’re saving hundreds of dollars. But then the rest of their gear is up to 50% off, such as 30% off their big RangeBuster batteries.
Check out
all of the sales here
The awesomeness of JackRabbit’s Micro-bikes is a micro-hill I’m prepared to die on, and I definitely recommend these models to anyone who wants a compact electric two-wheeler that rides as stable as a typical Class 2 e-bike but can fold flat to fit in a tiny space like behind a couch or under a dorm room bed.
I’m never parting with my own JackRabbit, and I love seeing new riders discover just how much fun these awesomely strange bikes are!
Mod Bikes
Austin, Texas-based Mod Bikes doesn’t get as much press as some of the larger players, but I think they deserve a second look for several reasons. Not only are they continuously pushing out new and impressive bikes as well as cool technology alongside them (don’t forget about their locking
streetside charging stands for e-bikes!
), but they also have cool rides that no one else has managed to create.
Case in point: The Mod Easy Sidecar e-bike that looks like a million bucks, but costs
just $3,495
after the $400 deal for Black Friday. I love this e-bike for riding around with my nephews as well as the family dog, which you can see below.
There’s even a
Sahara version
of it that looks like it just got back from an incredible desert expedition!
Juiced Bikes
Juiced Bikes was
revived this year
, and the company is back with a vengeance! The high-performance bikes are better than ever, and
the prices are bette
The recently launched Scrambler Mini leads the pack in pricing,
starting at just $949
thanks to its Black Friday promotional price. That’d be an awesome model for any young riders this season. But the larger versions are also pushing the value war forward with their own great sales.
There’s a lot to like here, from higher-end parts to 5-year warranties to the backing of the nation’s largest e-bike company, Lectric eBikes. Basically, it’s hard to imagine finding a better deal on a moto-style electric bike these days than from Juiced.
VMAX electric scooters
Sure, e-bikes are my first love, but electric scooters absolutely deserve their place in the micromobility ecosystem thanks to their extreme portability and compact, space-saving size.
VMAX is my favorite electric scooter company, which brings its Swiss design to the US and European scooter markets. When it came to putting my nephew on a scooter to get to school, I made sure he had a VMAX VX2 Lite to cruise around safely and securely. That scooter is marked down
to just $639
for Black Friday, despite offering impressive performance of 25 mph (40 km/h) and over 50 miles (80 km) of range!
I reviewed that scooter
recently and can tell you that the price is more than worth it!
The new VX4 is a 37 mph (60 km/h) model that is on sale for
just $1,199,
though you can get the previous version of that scooter with slightly more muted performance for an even better price of
There are a lot of great deals to be had, and you can see all of
VMAX’s sales here
Any more I should add?
These are the major sales that jumped out at me, but let me know what other sales you’ve seen on e-bikes you recommend.
I’ll take a look too and update if I see something I know I can stand behind. There are a lot of great e-bikes out there, and having ridden so many by now, I love being able to share my experiences, especially when there’s a good deal to be had at the end!

title: If I could only use one bike lock, it'd be this: FoldyLock Elite 110 review
content:
security
Micah Toll
| Nov 26 2026 - 2:22 am PT
I ride e-bikes professionally, regularly testing new bikes and biking gear. I don’t even own a car – I get around almost exclusively on two wheels. So when it comes to important gear like bike locks for my fleet of e-bikes, I’ve become pretty well-versed out of necessity. And after testing out the world’s strongest folding lock, the
FoldyLock Elite 110
, I’m more than impressed. If I could only have one lock for my e-bikes, it’d be this one.
Of course, the name of the game in bike theft prevention is to use more than just one lock, and I’m going to return to that idea at the end of this article.
But for now, believe me when I say that this lock is seriously good, to the point that it has become my new primary.
As long and strong as high-quality chain locks, but lighter, quieter, and more compact!
The FoldyLock Elite 110cm is identical in strength and security to the FoldyLock Forever 90cm that
I tested
a few years ago, yet is 20 cm (8 inches) longer, reaching 110 cm (43 inches).
The FoldyLock Forever 90 and FoldyLock Elite 110 are the strongest folding locks in the world, confirmed by the premier international lock certification organization ART. These are the only folding locks that have ever achieved a 3-star ART certification. The scale goes up to 5, but 4-star and 5-star certifications are motorcycle-level locks.
To make things even more impressive, the FoldyLock line achieved that ART 3-star rating three years ago, and no other lock company has matched it on a folding lock since.
If one independent and international lock testing association isn’t enough for you, the lock is also Sold Secure GOLD rated, which is just one step below Sold Secure’s highest ever rating for bike locks.
Again, more on that at the end of this article to get you to that last step for top security.
Why a folding lock?
There are a lot of different styles of locks out there, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. But as someone who rides e-bikes every day as his job, I’ve come to the opinion that a strong folding lock has the best combination of maximizing advantages and minimizing disadvantages.
For starters, folding locks allow you to lock to larger diameter anchors that would be impossible for U-locks (trees, telephone poles, multiple fence bars, etc). They’re more compact than chain locks of comparable security, both in size and weight. They’re significantly stronger than cable locks (when made with quality materials). And they mount more easily to a bike frame than nearly any other lock style, as they fold tightly and usually come with a holster.
Yes, there are disadvantages too. The segments mean they can’t form as close to a circle as a chain, meaning the maximum size of the tree or telephone pole you’re locking to is slightly smaller than for an equal length chain. And they usually aren’t quite as strong as U-Locks made with angle-grinder-resistant materials. But for their size and convenience, they make perhaps the best single style of lock for the best pairing of strength and convenience.
The concrete foundation kept the bike too far away for a U-lock, but the FoldyLock Elite had no problem reaching multiple fence bars
But why the FoldyLock Elite 110 specifically?
Since I began testing the
FoldyLock Elite 110
, I’ve been living with it as my main e-bike lock. I test a lot of locks, and most go onto the shelf when I’m done as backups or to give to friends/family. But the FoldyLock Elite 110 has stayed as my new primary lock, and here’s why.
First of all, as I mentioned, it’s the strongest folding lock in the world, as confirmed by multiple independent testing organizations. So if you want the advantages of a folding lock, there’s simply none more secure than this.
But beyond that, the FoldyLock Elite 110 is covered by multiple patents, including the specialized protected rivets that prevent nut splitter attacks and that take out any squeaks or rattles that are common in other folding locks. The lock also physically locks into its holster, which keeps it both secure (no bounce-outs) and helps keep it silent during the ride. There’s even a coating on the hardened steel segments to protect my bike frame from scratches and resist corrosion during winter use (plus a shutter on the locking mechanism for additional winter corrosion resistance).
Basically, it seems like the company has taken pretty much all of the learnings from previous locks in their lineup, and applied those lessons to the FoldyLock Elite, making it a perfect combination of strength, security, and convenience.
For these scenarios, the only high-security lock options are a chain or a folding lock
How do I use the lock?
As I mentioned, after my time testing the FoldyLock Elite, I can say for sure that if I could only use one bike lock, it would be this one.
But I don’t just use one bike lock. And I recommend you don’t either, if you can swing it.
We’ve long known that the best way to keep your bike safe from thieves is to use two bike locks. It’s partly for the extra security, and partly for the extra time it takes a thief to work on defeating two locks, meaning they’re more likely to choose a different sucker’s bike to steal.
I always recommend using two different styles of bike locks. Think: folding lock plus U-lock, or U-lock plus chain lock, or chain lock plus cable lock, or cable lock plus folding lock, etc. You get the idea.
My FoldyLock Elite is now my primary lock, and it allows me to lock onto just about everything on the street, from official bike racks to chunky utility poles. For my secondary, I use a
SeatyLock Mason 220
. This U-lock is actually one step higher-rated by Sold Secure, reaching that testing organization’s Diamond level – its highest level of security rating.
Two good locks are better than one!
When I can lock both the folding lock and U-lock to an anchor, I do it. But sometimes, when I’m forced to lock to something wide like a lamppost, I lock the frame and rear wheel with the FoldyLock Elite 110, then lock the front wheel to the frame with the
Mason 220 U-lock
, as seen in the photo above.
That keeps both of my wheels and my bike locked. Despite there only being one lock keeping the bike in place to the anchor (lamppost), the second lock adds an extra layer of frustration for a thief and is likely to convince them to just choose the next bike on the sidewalk.
That’s why I always recommend using two different locks, and ideally of different styles. I believe the FoldyLock Elite 110 offers the most advantages, but its few disadvantages are offset by a secondary lock, such as a strong U-lock.
When it comes to mounting, I’ve got the holster mounted onto my fork using the supplied flexible mounting straps.
Normally you’d mount it to one of your bottle mounts, but I only have a single set of bottle bosses on my e-bike’s frame, and they are currently taken up by a water bottle holder (surprise!).
I found that despite adding 1.9 kg or 4.1 lb to the side of my fork, my bike still rides just fine. The advantage of a rigid frame is that there’s not really much change to the unsprung mass since everything is unsprung!
I love riding hands-free in the city, and it did take me a day or two to get used to the slightly altered steering moment, but I can still ride my bike hands-free even with the extra weight there on the side of the fork.
At some point I might shift the holster onto the rear rack or swap it out for my bottle holder in favor of a new bottle spot, but so far it’s working great there and hasn’t caused me any handling issues.
Is the FoldyLock Elite 110 worth it?
When it comes to value, I think the FoldyLock Elite 110 takes the cake here, too. It’s normally priced at
an MSRP of $145
, though it’s currently
on sale for $119
as part of the Black Friday promotions.
There are many diverging rules of thumb out there regarding how much a lock should cost, often landing at around 10-20% of the cost of your bike. I don’t subscribe to any of those fixed numbers, as it all depends on how much you want to keep your bike, but considering this lock is likely to outlast even your nicest e-bikes for several years, I’d say that even the full price of $145 feels like a steal compared to other top-tier locks that go for $200 or more.
As I said, I test hundreds of bikes and dozens of locks as my day job. I live and breathe bikes. The fact that this lock has become my go-to everyday lock is pretty much all you need to know about how impressive it truly is. It’s a pleasure to live with and use, which means that I actually end up using it.

title: Gambia signs four solar PPAs totalling 232 MW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The Gambia’s state-owned utility has inked four large-scale solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) since late October, with battery storage included in each project.
Patrick Jowett
26 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
The Gambia’s state-owned National Water and Electricity Company (NAWEC) has entered into four solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) within the last month, with battery storage included in each project.
The largest agreement, signed in late October, covers a planned 148.44 MW solar project with a 50 MW/200 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS). The project will be built in Soma, in the country’s Lower River Region.
Under the 25-year PPA, NAWEC will act as the sole offtaker. The project is being developed by Gambian-based renewable energy company Solaris Africa Ltd.
NAWEC signed a second PPA last week with the AEE-HGR consortium, a clean-energy partnership between pan-African contractor AEE Power and independent power producer HGR Energy. The agreement covers a 52 MW solar power plant, also in Soma, alongside 40.9 MWh of battery storage.
A separate government implementation agreement was signed during the ceremony. The project will connect to the 225 kV regional transmission infrastructure near Soma, allowing electricity to be fed directly into the national grid.
Last Friday, NAWEC signed a PPA with Türkiye-based developer Agata Energy for a 21.33 MW solar plant paired with 20 MWh of battery storage, according to details published by local media. The duration of the agreement has not yet been disclosed.
The project is planned for Farafenni, in the Gambia’s North Bank Region, where it is expected to strengthen electricity supply and grid stability.
The most recent agreement is between NAWEC and Gambian solar energy company SolarTech, covering a 10.4 MW solar project with 4 MWh of battery storage in Gunjur, in the country’s West Coast Region. The developer says the PPA has a 25-year term.
Together, these four agreements cover 232.17 MW of proposed solar capacity and 264.9 MWh of battery storage. Further project details, including indicative construction and commissioning timeframes, have yet to be released.
Once operational, the projects will considerably increase The Gambia’s installed solar capacity. According to the Africa Solar Industry Association’s (AFSIA) project database, the country’s largest operational solar project is the 23 MW Jambur solar plant, tied to 20 MW/8 MWh of battery storage. The plant was commissioned in
March 2024
AFSIA’s database has tracked a total 101.1 MW of operational solar in the Gambia, the majority of which is listed as unidentified C&I projects.
The government of the Gambia has set a target of reaching 30% renewable energy in its generation mix by 2030. In 2024, the share of renewables sat at around 13%, when including imports. The country is also working towards achieving universal electricity access by 2030, up from around 73% in 2024, according to World Bank figures.

title: Norwegian IPP shifts South African solar project to corporate buyers - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Norwegian independent power producer (IPP) Scatec said it plans to withdraw a 288 MW solar project from South Africa’s public renewables procurement program and sell it into the country’s growing corporate power market instead.
Brian Publicover
26 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Scatec said on Nov. 26 that it has decided to withdraw its 288 MW Mercury solar project from South Africa’s Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme (REIPPPP) and sell it to Lyra Energy, its joint venture supplying commercial and industrial customers under multi-year power purchase agreements (PPAs).
The Norwegian company cited “growing demand for corporate offtake agreements at attractive returns.” Lyra expects to start construction on Mercury in the first half of 2027. Scatec did not disclose the sale price.
South Africa’s Department of Electricity and Energy listed Mercury Solar PV 2, developed by Scatec Solar Africa, as a
preferred bidder in REIPPPP Bid Window 7
, with a contracted capacity of 240 MW at a tariff of ZAR 486.86/MWh in Free State province. Scatec did not explain the difference between that figure and the 288 MW cited in its announcement, and it did not say whether the withdrawal has been finalized with the government.
Lyra has also reached financial close on the 126 MW Noko solar project, and Scatec has started construction. Scatec will contribute about $13 million in equity and expects about $100 million in design and construction revenue. Standard Bank will provide non-recourse debt. Commercial operation is expected in the first half of 2028. Scatec did not disclose the project’s location or total cost.
Platform growth
Lyra, now owned 50/50 by Scatec and STANLIB Infrastructure Investments, buys Scatec-developed projects and moves them to construction once it has secured enough corporate offtake. It has 381 MW under construction across Noko and the 255 MW Thakadu project, which reached financial close in March, plus Mercury in its backlog.
Scatec CEO Terje Pilskog said Noko is “the second project being realized through the Lyra platform,” adding that Scatec is “creating value in a highly capital efficient way through our integrated business model in this deregulating market.”
South Africa’s private power market has expanded alongside public procurement. In February, SOLA Group closed financing on Naos-1, described as the country’s
largest private utility-scale solar and battery project
, which pairs 300 MW of PV with 660 MWh of storage to
wheel power to industrial customers
across the national grid. On the public side, solar approved under Bid Window 7, including three additional allocations,
stood close to 5 GW
as of July, and the country’s cumulative solar capacity exceeds 10 GW.

title: Rare periods of low PV generation can be managed with storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin) says that batteries could help manage shortfalls in solar and wind generation, while underground storage of green hydrogen could provide backup during prolonged periods of low renewable output.
Ralph Diermann,
Sandra Enkhardt
26 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Energy Storage
DIW Berlin researchers have examined how often periods of very low wind and solar generation have occurred and how electricity systems based entirely on renewable energy could manage them.
Claudia Kemfert, head of DIW Berlin’s Energy, Transport and Environment department, said at the opening of the Forum Solar Plus event in Berlin that the study proposes a definition of prolonged periods of low renewable generation for the first time. She added that such periods could last longer than previously assumed.
Kemfert also said Germany would need sustainable biomass to help cover these periods, alongside a significantly faster expansion of solar and wind power.
The DIW analysis shows that short periods of low renewable generation occur relatively frequently. An assessment of conditions between 1982 and 2019 found that combined solar, onshore wind and offshore wind generation in Germany fell to half of installed capacity an average of 112 times per year for 12-hour periods and 24 times per year for 24-hour periods. Batteries can help manage these shorter periods.
Hydrogen
The DIW researchers consider prolonged periods of low renewable generation more challenging, although they occur very rarely. Complementary generation from solar and wind installations ensures that some renewable capacity remains available. The geographic distribution of generation also helps mitigate the effects, as fluctuations in renewable power output can partly offset one another across larger areas and national borders. Electricity trading with neighboring countries can therefore help manage periods of low generation, provided sufficient cross-border transmission capacity is available.
However, long-duration electricity storage is also needed to cover extreme periods of low renewable generation. The DIW researchers propose building storage facilities for green hydrogen that can be converted back into electricity when needed. Such facilities could store large quantities of energy over extended periods and shift renewable electricity generated in summer to winter.
Germany currently has initial small-scale demonstration and research facilities for underground hydrogen storage in salt caverns, with capacities in the gigawatt-hour range, either operating or under construction. Other European countries, particularly the United Kingdom and Austria, are further advanced. Across the countries examined by DIW Berlin, planned underground storage facilities have a combined capacity of almost 90 TWh.
That would not be sufficient, however. In a medium scenario that accounts for planned expansion of Europe’s electricity and hydrogen networks, the analysis estimates that 170 TWh of storage capacity would be needed across the countries studied. Under an extreme weather scenario comparable to the 55-day period of low renewable generation in the winter of 1996–1997, the most severe such event since 1982, the requirement would rise to 350 TWh.
State support
The DIW researchers consider hydrogen storage infrastructure on this scale technically and practically feasible. They point out that Europe already stores a comparable volume of natural gas underground.
Planning and construction of hydrogen salt caverns would take around five to 15 years, depending on whether existing natural gas storage facilities are converted or new hydrogen storage facilities are built. DIW energy economist Wolf-Peter Schill said investment decisions should therefore be made soon.
The researchers note that holding storage capacity for extreme periods of low renewable generation is unlikely to be commercially attractive to private investors because it would probably be used at full capacity only very rarely. Schill therefore argues that targeted risk-mitigation and support mechanisms are needed. He says long-duration electricity storage should also be considered in the design of the comprehensive capacity mechanism planned for 2032, which is intended to ensure sufficient firm power capacity during periods of tight electricity supply.

title: Spain could reach 10 GW of batteries by 2030, but bankability remains the major challenge - pv magazine Global
content: Spain could have between 6 GW and 10 GW of battery energy storage by the end of 2030, according to estimates presented during the roundtable “How can Spain make its batteries bankable?” organized by pv magazine on Nov. 25 at the Genera 2026 trade fair at IFEMA Madrid. Participants included Luis Marquina, president of the Spanish Energy Storage Business Association (AEPIBAL); Carlos Jerez, head of structured finance at BNZ; Iker Labiano, head of energy storage systems (ESS) for Spain and Portugal at Sungrow; and Javier Revuelta, vice president of power and renewables consulting at Wood Mackenzie. “We estimate between 6 and 8 GW, and we lean more toward 8 than 6,” Marquina said of the installation outlook through the end of the decade. For his part, Jerez said of the projects Sungrow has under development in Spain , all of them hybridization projects, will be installed within that timeframe. Labiano noted that in 2027 alone, storage equipment with a capacity exceeding 10 GWh could arrive in Spain, noting that another six to eight months can pass between battery delivery and grid connection. Revuelta raised the forecast to 10 GW by 2030, equivalent to slightly under 40 GWh, given that not all projects will have a four-hour duration. “I think nobody in Spain builds a PV plant without hybridizing it, or at least without trying,” said the consultant, who believes the combination of hybridizations of existing installations, new solar plants, and standalone storage projects will make it possible to reach that figure. The evolution of electricity demand, data center deployment, the future of nuclear power plants, gas prices, and self-consumption will be among the variables determining the sector’s pace of growth, alongside reductions in the levelized cost of storage (LCOS). Revuelta highlighted in particular the potential for extending battery lifespans, which could increase from roughly 8,000 cycles today to 15,000 in the coming years. “At the same CAPEX, 15,000 cycles is practically half the LCOS,” he explained. Cannibalization of battery revenues The entry of new storage capacity will create a scenario of growing competition for specific revenue streams. “What gets cannibalized are revenue streams,” Marquina clarified, estimating that the secondary regulation market, currently one of the main sources of battery profitability, has the capacity to absorb between 1.5 GW and 2 GW of storage. “We believe it is a market that will decline very rapidly over a two- to three-year horizon,” he added. The AEPIBAL president was more optimistic about arbitrage in the day-ahead market, driven by price spreads generated by the addition of large volumes of solar power without a corresponding rise in electricity demand. The association estimates that this spread will remain at a minimum of €70/MWh over the next 10 years. Regarding the hurdles to bringing Spain’s large pipeline of storage projects under development to fruition, Marquina pointed out that a significant share of initiatives will not even reach the financing stage due to administrative bottlenecks, social acceptance issues, or coordination problems with grid connection infrastructure. Once past that stage, project viability will depend on the ability to structure revenues through power purchase agreements (PPAs), tolling agreements, and other mechanisms that combine multiple remuneration streams. One of the most frequent mistakes in financial modeling, according to Marquina, is underestimating execution and connection timelines. “You set a timing, and the schedule is usually one of the mistakes,” he warned, referring to the financial impact a one-year delay can have once batteries have already been procured. The complexity of financing a dispatchable asset Jerez agreed on the importance of timelines, especially in hybridization projects at renewable facilities that already have project finance in place, where existing contracts must be made compatible with those of the new storage system. The BNZ executive noted that modeling battery revenues requires a far higher degree of customization than conventional solar assets. “The providers of the famous curves no longer work for everyone; instead, you have to carry out much more specific studies,” he explained, pointing to factors such as potential curtailment at the connection node. “That is where banks are particularly putting their focus, on the revenue side, how they are going to work and how credible they are,” Jerez added. On top of this is the need to coordinate supply contracts, existing PPAs, and long-term service and maintenance agreements for the batteries. According to Jerez, Spanish lenders are building experience with these assets, in some cases drawing on expertise from their teams in other markets. Even so, significant educational work remains. “It is a path we are walking together, developers and financial institutions,” he said. Revuelta, meanwhile, questioned the tendency to classify storage projects as simply bankable or non-bankable without considering the different levels of leverage each investment can support. In his view, while lenders tend to size debt based on contractually guaranteed revenues, equity investors can take on greater market exposure. “What you need to have, I believe, is a map of scenarios and not bet everything on red or black,” he said. “If it only works for you in one, equity is going to tell you no.” Revuelta believes projects with different financing structures will coexist, including some developed entirely on balance sheet. “There are going to be banks that are very conservative, but there are going to be many projects that move forward with what I call brave equity.” Arbitrage could account for 80% of revenues The composition of battery income, known as revenue stacking, will evolve as installed storage capacity grows and new services are developed for the power system. According to Marquina, in 2026 secondary regulation is providing roughly 60% of revenues, compared to 40% from arbitrage. Over the long term, however, arbitrage could come to represent around 80%. The AEPIBAL president called for remuneration of the services that batteries can provide to the electricity system but that do not yet carry financial compensation. “The regulator has to enable all the services that add value to the power system; they have to be remunerated, and that still means there is revenue ground to cover from a regulatory standpoint,” he said. Optimizing different revenue streams will also require careful management of equipment and degradation. Marquina noted that in certain projects, deviations of up to 15% have been observed between actual battery performance and the assumptions used in business models. From the manufacturers’ perspective, Labiano underscored the importance of supplier solvency when closing financing. “We are seeing that for banks, the bankability of the company, of the supplier, is fundamental,” said the Sungrow executive. Labiano estimates that standalone projects account for around 20% of storage developments in Spain, despite their revenue-generating potential. “Most developments are hybrids, hybrids associated fundamentally with solar,” he explained, noting that four hours is the predominant duration due to the characteristics of Spain’s residual demand curve. Marquina drew a distinction between hybrid projects with and without grid-charging capability. “Without grid charging, we maintain that it is an investment that saves solar PV right off the bat and is also very good in itself,” he said. The ability to charge from the grid, however, expands options for participating in electricity markets and prevents battery availability from depending solely on solar generation. The capacity market: between system needs and competition Panelists also debated the design of Spain’s future capacity market and the weight it will carry in financing batteries. Revuelta questioned the approach of some developers who plug an estimate of future capacity payments into their financial models and then assess whether their investments are profitable. “The capacity market does not work like that; it works the other way around,” he said. According to the consultant, the starting point must be the power system’s firm capacity needs, as determined by resource adequacy studies. If the system needs a given volume of storage, capacity remuneration will have to help ensure the necessary investments materialize. “There is another question, which is how much the system needs, because if 3 GW are profitable and the system needs 10, 3 will not come, 10 will come,” he argued. Marquina qualified this view, noting that the competitive nature of auctions will ultimately determine remuneration and that system capacity needs do not guarantee any individual project will win an award. “The system is not going to set a price; it is going to set capacity needs, and the price will be made by those who submit bids,” he said. The presence of grant-backed projects with different investment costs and return expectations could increase competitive pressure on clearing prices. “You can find yourself submitting a very good bid, only to be undercut by a wide margin and left out,” Marquina added. From a financing standpoint, Jerez noted that unlike Italy’s MACSE mechanism, capacity payments in Spain are expected to represent a minority share of battery revenues. “If you ask a financial institution, its dream scenario is 100% capacity payments. That is very bankable, as has been seen in Italy,” he said, noting that the Italian model allows leverage levels of up to 90% of CAPEX. In Spain, lenders will have to accept greater exposure to merchant revenues and understand the shift from conventional renewable generation assets to dispatchable assets. “Previously, we started from plants that you simply plugged in and they generated when the resource was there. Now we have moved to a scenario in which where you can shift those megawatt-hours is what will allow you to optimize and get the most out of the investments,” Jerez explained. Lenders can also turn to accelerated debt-repayment mechanisms, such as cash sweeps, to protect against a potential drop in revenues and equipment wear resulting from more intensive cycling strategies in the early years. Tolling agreements and the rescue of solar PV Marquina noted that tolling agreements with creditworthy counterparties could allow leverage levels above 80% in storage projects using Tier 1 equipment and suppliers. These agreements, in which a counterparty acquires certain commercial dispatch rights to the battery in exchange for contractual remuneration, also introduce new questions regarding asset operation, cycling, and degradation. Revuelta expects hybridizations to dominate the Spanish market by volume due to the financial difficulties facing part of the solar PV fleet installed in recent years. Adding batteries can improve revenues at these plants, provided the storage system can generate enough return to pay back its own investment and add incremental value to the solar asset. Not all lenders, however, will be willing to increase exposure to projects already struggling to meet their debt obligations. “It is going to be difficult to go to the parent company and say: ‘Hey, this is a project that is doing poorly, but if we put in more money, in principle it will be better,’” Revuelta said. Marquina described adding storage as a technical fix for the economic challenges facing the solar sector. “Hybridization is the technical rescue by definition,” he said. The need to make additional investments and acquire new asset-management capabilities could also spur M&A activity in Spain’s renewable energy market. “PV is the simplest technology of all existing technologies. And now we are moving to a dispatchable asset model; it has a different level of complexity,” Marquina said. The AEPIBAL president noted that some developers are looking for buyers capable of taking on this second phase of asset development. Revuelta believes 2028 and 2029 could be particularly difficult for certain solar projects if high PV penetration, lower gas prices, and still-insufficient battery deployment coincide. In that scenario, some lenders may be forced to restructure debt or facilitate the sale of plants to investors with the capacity to hybridize them. The consultant also questioned whether it makes sense to systematically rely on tolling agreements to finance batteries co-located with solar plants, noting that such contracts carry an opportunity cost. “The battery is already the hedge for PV. A hedge usually costs money,” he explained. The decision will depend on balancing the upside forgone in exchange for contractual certainty against the benefits of accessing bank debt. “There is not going to be one situation that is the case everyone will follow,” Revuelta concluded. Gas prices and future price spreads Developments in international gas markets will be another factor shaping storage profitability in Spain. Revuelta anticipates a major expansion in global liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply between now and 2030, driven primarily by the United States, which could put strong downward pressure on prices. “It is very difficult to stay in sync; what happens with electricity also happens in the gas or oil world, where investment cycles are not always aligned with demand,” he explained. The consultant pointed to the 2028–2030 window as a particularly delicate period for renewable generation if cheaper gas, higher solar capacity, and delays in storage deployment and demand electrification converge. He acknowledged, however, that geopolitical events or supply disruptions could significantly alter that outlook. A drop in gas prices would affect battery discharge prices, though rising CO2 emission allowance costs could partially offset that effect on combined-cycle gas turbine generation costs. Marquina stressed the importance of the spread between electricity purchase and sale prices. “With the spread, you have to see whether it is at 70 or at 40. At 70 it holds up. At 40 it is going to suffer, of course,” he said. Revuelta believes the electrification of transport and heating and cooling, along with backup needs stemming from the evolution of the nuclear fleet, will ensure a market for batteries beyond the next decade. Safety, warranties, and maintenance contracts From a technical perspective, Labiano identified safety and the ability to provide maintenance services throughout a battery’s lifespan as key elements a manufacturer must deliver to facilitate financing. “The first and fundamental thing is to find a supplier, a manufacturer, that gives you that safety. And then, also important, that gives you service—that if there is a failure, if you have a problem over the life of a battery, they resolve it for you,” he explained. The Sungrow executive highlighted the need for lenders to understand the scope of long-term service agreements (LTSAs), as well as the risks covered by manufacturer warranties. “Even within the sector there is still no established language; there are things that are taken for granted that are not there,” he warned. “The job of the bank or the bank’s advisors must be that: to understand exactly what is being bought, what is going to be built, and what risks that entails.” Labiano stressed that the equipment sold in Spain is essentially the same as that supplied in Italy, Poland, France, or Germany, meaning differences in how these markets develop are largely driven by their respective remuneration frameworks. “We need solutions so that the revenue is clearer,” he said. Marquina noted that according to AEPIBAL estimates, Spain’s capacity market could account for only 10% to 15% of battery revenues, resulting in a business model substantially different from Italy’s. Revuelta expressed confidence that the technical needs of the power system will ultimately drive the introduction of a capacity mechanism, regardless of political developments. “In all scenarios, between a lot and a huge amount of batteries are needed,” he said. Nuclear continuity and data centers Panelists also examined the potential impact of extending the operating life of Spain’s nuclear power plants on storage profitability. Revuelta warned that a nuclear phase-out would not necessarily be positive for arbitrage: while it would increase backup needs, it could also reduce the frequency of zero-price hours and raise battery charging costs. “If you remove 7 GW of nuclear, maybe half of the zero-price hours disappear,” he explained. “You have to run the numbers. It is not trivial.” Demand growth from data centers introduces another major variable of uncertainty into forecasts. Revuelta believes Spain could add up to 15 GW of additional demand from data centers between now and 2040, though how much ultimately materializes remains difficult to predict. Marquina cautioned that the load profile of these facilities does not always match the flat consumption pattern typically attributed to them. “Their demand is neither as flat nor as beneficial as is claimed. They generate a lot of distortion for the system,” he said. Integrating batteries at data centers may therefore serve not only an economic optimization strategy, but also power stability and supply quality needs. Four hours consolidates as the standard On the duration of storage systems currently in demand in Spain, panelists agreed that four hours has become the dominant configuration. “Right now it is all four hours,” Labiano said, recalling that four or five years ago Sungrow developed one of its first one-hour projects in Spain. Marquina attributed part of this shift to the design of public grant programs, which helped establish four hours as a benchmark for the sector and led some developers to redesign projects originally planned for two hours. Revuelta explained that this duration also reflects electricity market price structures. “There are going to be eight cheap hours, but let’s say only four very expensive hours. So hour five, hour six, and hour seven start to have a tiny spread,” he said. Further reductions in equipment costs could pave the way for six- or eight-hour projects. Jerez added that optimal battery sizing will also depend on land availability, grid connection conditions, and potential curtailment at each node. The BNZ executive also emphasized the need for greater visibility on flexible demand access rules and the effective ability of storage facilities to charge from the grid. “People are moving forward with permits, but a key part is: hey, can this charge from the grid, yes or no, and when?” he said. The answer to that question will shape the ability to monetize assets, negotiate long-term hedging agreements, and ultimately structure financing. The particularities of the Spanish market The predominance of hybridizations over standalone projects is one of the main differences between Spain’s storage market and other European markets such as Germany, Italy, or the United Kingdom. Marquina rejected the idea that this particularity should be viewed as a disadvantage. “It is an opportunity. Each market has its own dynamics and characteristics,” he said, pointing to Spain’s strong solar and wind resources and available land for renewable development. Revuelta attributed the situation to the mismatch between the pace of solar PV deployment and battery rollouts. “We moved very fast, too fast, I would say, with solar, and we started a bit late with batteries,” he said. The consultant recalled that just three years ago, storage business cases looked less attractive, and that solar penetration and the frequency of zero-price hours have exceeded many market expectations. This has been compounded by longer-than-expected permitting timelines for battery projects. “Everyone expected the first batteries to be permitted for connection in 2024, and we are in 2026 and we have zero-point-something gigawatts,” he said. Another particularity of the Spanish market is the merchant exposure of a portion of its solar fleet, compared with other European countries where assets rely more heavily on PPAs or contracts for difference (CfDs). Labiano also highlighted the different commercial conditions facing battery manufacturers. “If the saying is ‘Spain is different,’ I completely agree in this case, in the case of batteries,” he said. The Sungrow executive pointed to heavier price pressure on equipment in Spain and the fact that storage projects deliver higher returns in other markets. Revuelta likewise noted that certain services remunerated in Germany or the UK, such as primary frequency response, are mandatory and unremunerated in Spain. The lack of these additional revenue streams leaves Spanish storage more heavily reliant on electricity market price spreads. From grid connection permit to bankable project In the final stretch of the discussion, panelists identified the main factors separating a viable storage project from one that merely holds grid access and connection capacity. Marquina pointed to administrative delays, a lack of regulatory consistency across Spain’s autonomous communities, and the absence of sufficiently established construction and safety standards. “We have gone from projects that should take 18 months to 36 months now, and we are heading toward 48. And this is a problem,” he warned. Revuelta identified the lack of a revenue track record as one of the main barriers to bank financing. Unlike a conventional PV plant, whose revenues depend primarily on solar irradiance and power prices, a battery’s profitability is closely tied to the quality of its commercial and operational management. “Two PV plants generate very similar money, but two batteries in the hands of different people generate very different money,” he explained. Until lenders have a sufficient track record on optimizer revenues and equipment degradation, a substantial portion of financing will continue to rely on projections. Revuelta argued in favor of financing merchant-exposed projects using conservative assumptions and sufficiently high debt service coverage ratios (DSCRs), rather than excluding uncontracted revenues from financial models altogether. “Start from the most conservative one, add another cushion on top with a debt service coverage ratio of 2 or 2.5, and that allows you to put in quite a bit more debt,” he said, referring to forecasts prepared by different consultancies. Labiano recalled that in the UK, several years also passed between the installation of the first batteries and their access to bank financing. Jerez added that current challenges must also be viewed in the context of refinancing Spain’s existing solar fleet and the higher cost of capital compared with when many of those assets were originally financed. “A large share of the projects were financed with Euribor at zero or close to zero, and now you have Euribor above 3%,” he noted. Labiano believes developers able to anticipate how the market evolves will be the ones to capture today’s storage opportunities. “There really are people—I would say CEOs or companies, entrepreneurs—who have a vision and bet on it, run the numbers, take more or less risk, are more or less conservative, and they are the first ones developing,” he said. Marquina closed with a warning about the risks of using low-quality equipment, both for plant safety and for the social acceptance of storage. “This business, as it stands today, for reasons of social license, financing, and permitting, leaves no room for products that are not Tier 1,” he said. According to the AEPIBAL president, that standard must extend across the entire value chain, including EPC contractors, optimizers, advisors, and equipment suppliers. Despite regulatory, financial, and commercial uncertainties, Revuelta concluded that Spain’s storage market is still in its infancy and that battery demand will not end with the first wave of installations. “We are at the very beginning of an S-curve that, moreover, is not going to be just those five years, as some think, and then it’s over,” the consultant said. “I see 10 GW in 2030, but no less than 30 GW in 2050.” The post Spain could reach 10 GW of batteries by 2030, but bankability remains the major challenge appeared first on pv magazine Global .

title: India adds 11.2 GW of rooftop PV capacity in first nine months of 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
India’s residential segment accounted for more than 95% of rooftop solar additions in the third quarter of 2026, driven by the government’s PM Surya Ghar program. Cumulative installed rooftop PV capacity reached 32 GW by the end of September.
Uma Gupta
26 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Highlights
Residential
A residential solar installation by SolarSquare
India installed 4.7 GW of rooftop solar capacity in the third quarter of 2026, up 124% from 2.1 GW a year earlier, according to Mercom India’s newly released “Q3 and 9M 2026 India Rooftop Solar Market Report.” Rooftop solar accounted for more than 42% of the country’s total solar capacity additions during the quarter.
Residential installations continued to drive rooftop solar growth, accounting for 95.2% of quarterly additions. Industrial, commercial, and government installations accounted for 2.5%, 1.7%, and 0.6%, respectively.
The capital expenditure (capex) model accounted for 92% of rooftop solar installations in the third quarter, while the operational expenditure (opex)/renewable energy service company (RESCO) model accounted for 8%.
Uttar Pradesh led quarterly installations with a 17% share, followed by Maharashtra (15%) and Gujarat (13%).
India added 11.2 GW of rooftop solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, up 129% from 4.9 GW in the corresponding period of 2025. Residential installations accounted for approximately 9.9 GW, followed by industrial and commercial installations at 800 MW and 500 MW, respectively.
The country’s cumulative installed rooftop solar capacity reached 32 GW at the end of September 2026.
The government’s PM Surya Ghar program continues to drive rooftop solar growth, with nearly 5.95 million households installing rooftop PV systems by the end of September. Another 3.7 million applications were pending, representing an estimated residential rooftop solar pipeline of 10.96 GW, based on an average system size of 3 kW.
According to the report, domestic content requirements (DCR) and the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) are increasingly influencing procurement and project decisions. Limited availability of DCR-compliant modules, higher prices, advance booking requirements, and longer delivery times are affecting project completion.
“PM Surya Ghar has changed the scale of India’s residential rooftop solar market and is the driving force behind record growth. With the current program scheduled to end in March 2027 and millions of applications still pending, the focus has to be on converting that demand into installations through faster financing, smoother DISCOM processes, better equipment availability, and a larger pool of qualified installers. There is also the need for early policy direction on PM Surya Ghar 2.0 so the market does not lose momentum and consumers, installers, and manufacturers can plan beyond the current program,” said Raj Prabhu, CEO of Mercom Capital Group.
Average rooftop solar system costs showed mixed trends in the third quarter of 2026, ranging from INR 29.7 ($0.32)/W for systems using Chinese monocrystalline PERC modules to INR 44.4/W for systems using Indian DCR-compliant TOPCon modules. DCR-compliant systems remained the most expensive.

title: Estonian solar park energized with 55 MW/250 MWh battery - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Project developers say the battery energy storage system, which is tied to a 77.5 MW solar farm operational from 2024, features the Baltics’ largest battery system by storage capacity to date.
Patrick Jowett
26 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Estonian energy company Evecon and French investment manager Mirova have added a 55 MW/250 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) to an operational 77.5 MW solar park.
The two companies say the project, located near the town of Lihula in western Estonia, features the largest capacity battery storage system in the Baltics and currently stands as the most powerful hybrid park in the region.
The 77.5 MW solar farm was completed in October 2024. Evecon and Mirova have since invested €110 million ($120.7 million) in bringing the project’s hybridization to completion, with the project developed through their joint venture Baltic Renewable Energy Platform (BREP).
Construction of the BESS started in January this year, with Tallinn-headquartered construction company WiSo Engineering acting as the main contractor. The company took responsibility for both building the infrastructure and integrating the storage system, having previously completed the Kirikmäe solar plant.

Dec. 1, 2026 at 3 .p.m CET
we will welcome
five industry experts
who will share their
first-hand experience
of developing, building and financing hybrid projects in
leading European markets.
Join us at
pv magazine Week Europe
for four days of dynamic discussion with industry leaders and experts, taking in co-location, quality, cybersecurity and other vital issues for renewable energy in Europe and beyond.
Register today.
WiSo Engineering Chief Executive Risto Virveste confirmed the battery storage system is technically complete, with the final grid and market tests now being finalized.
BREP entered into a ten-year flexibility and power purchase agreement (FPPA) with German energy company Pure Energy, covering the output of the hybrid system, as well BREP’s 15.5 MW Imavere and 12.8 MW Lohu Mets solar power plants. The agreement, first announced in February, is described as the first FPPA in the Baltics.
At the time, BREP also announced the completion of an €85 million long-term financing package from Swedish banking group Swedbank, that went towards the refinancing of its existing solar portfolio and the construction of the Kirikmäe BESS.
Evecon CEO Karl-Joonatan Kvell called the completed hybrid project “an important step towards increased Estonian energy security and an electricity system that relies more on local renewable energy”.
Estonia, alongside its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Lithuania, have managed grid frequency independently since desynchronizing from the Russian grid and synchronizing with continental Europe in February 2025.
Among the largest battery projects operational in Estonia is the
Hertz 2 BESS
, a 100 MW/200 MWh system, which was switched on in July. It stands next to the
Hertz 1 BESS
, of the same capacity, which opened in February.
In September, Finnish fund manager Taaleri Energia and Baltic private equity firm KJK Capital backed plans for a
192 MW/420 MWh battery
in Estonia. Construction started the same month, with the battery expected to be operational by November 2027.

title: Huawei launches Luterra S2 in Europe - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Luterra S2 uses 5 and 7 kWh battery modules featuring LFP technology and calls rated at 318 Ah. The 7 kWh module weighs 57 kg and provides 6.9 kWh of usable energy, while the 5 kWh module weighs 46 kg and provides 4.9 kWh. The system occupies 0.15 m2 of floor space and 0.69 m2 of wall space.
26 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Energy Storage
On November 9, Huawei launched LUTERRA S2, its new all-in-one residential energy storage solution, in Palma de Mallorca, Spain.  It integrates a hybrid inverter, storage, and AI-powered energy management in one stackable unit. Designed for easy deployment, LUTERRA S2 can be installed and commissioned in minutes. Available in single-phase (3-10 kW) and three-phase (5- 20 kW) configurations, LUTERRA S2 is the industry’s first all-in-one residential energy system built on Huawei’s proprietary full-SiC (silicon carbide) architecture, delivering exceptional efficiency, power density, and reliability.
Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business, officially introduced LUTERRA S2. During his presentation, he reviewed the evolution of residential systems, from split to integrated architectures and from AC coupling to DC coupling.
LUTERRA S2 combines a hybrid inverter and a modular energy storage system in a single residential solution. Huawei presented it as the industry’s first all-in-one residential system based on a Full-SiC MOS architecture. The company has brought SiC MOS technology, widely used in the automotive industry, to solar and energy storage applications, combining it with intelligent algorithms to improve efficiency while reducing the system’s size and weight.
Industrial design: an integrated architecture
Jules Parmentier, Director of Industrial Design Strategy and Innovation at Huawei, introduced LUTERRA S2’s industrial design. Inspired by the purity of Arctic landscapes and the beauty of sunlight, the all-in-one system combines a timeless monolithic design with an iconic, dynamic charge and discharge indicator.
To achieve a cleaner and more integrated appearance, Huawei relocated the heat dissipation structure to the rear of the unit and eliminated the plastic side covers of the modules. Ergonomics have also been improved through newly designed quick-release handles, facilitating the handling and installation of the battery modules. The entirely passive cooling system ensures quiet operation, with noise levels below 29 dB.
The FusionSolar app and user experience
Simon Ekstrand, Huawei’s Chief User-Centered Design (UCD) Expert, presented the design philosophy behind the LUTERRA S2 app. The interface uses dynamic visual elements to represent energy flows, illustrating exchanges between photovoltaic panels, the grid, the battery, the home and the electric vehicle.
The visualization adapts to the day-night cycle and weather conditions, making charging and discharging processes easier to understand. The app also provides natural-language explanations of how the system operates and how energy management decisions are made.
Among the new features is Cevia, an intelligent assistant that enables users to make complex queries using natural language and a visual interface based on dynamic cards. These features are integrated into FusionSolar app, allowing users to manage and monitor the system and access information about their installation’s energy performance.
Safety validation and partner participation
The event program included a presentation by Diego Becerro, a representative of TÜV Rheinland, focusing on safety validation. Huawei highlighted that its residential energy storage system had achieved the highest level of TÜV Rheinland’s Safety Mark certification.
LUTERRA S2 incorporates cell-level risk isolation mechanisms to prevent thermal runaway propagation, a directional channel for venting and cooling high-temperature gases, and continuous temperature monitoring at AC and DC connection points. If overheating is detected, the system automatically enters safe mode, activates LED alerts and sends notifications to the user.
Efficiency, safety, and ease of installation
Pablo Sánchez, Huawei’s Technical Director for Distributed Generation PV and Battery Storage, highlighted that the residential system delivers power outputs of up to 10 kW in single-phase configurations and 20 kW in three-phase configurations. The company estimates a cumulative energy delivery of 34,600 kWh over 15 years and states that the battery uses 318 Ah A+ grade cells.
The inverter incorporates Energy Boost technology, based on DTO packaging on SiC MOS, ANPC topology and high-frequency PWM algorithms. Its peak efficiency exceeds 99%, while the low-load algorithm enables efficiency levels above 98.5%. The system’s full charge-discharge round-trip efficiency (RTE) exceeds 90%.
The system also features Glacier Cooling, a technology that reduces total heat generation by 33% thanks to its Full-SiC power design. Meanwhile, Pin-fin technology increases thermal conductivity fivefold and expands the heat dissipation surface area by 90%.
In the area of energy management, Huawei introduced AI Scheduling 2.0, which uses Transformer and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to forecast photovoltaic generation and household demand and calculate charging and discharging strategies. More than 46,000 households are already using Huawei’s AI-powered energy scheduling solution, achieving an average revenue increase of more than 20%, according to figures presented during the event.
The installation process has been simplified into five stages: marking, base mounting, handling using integrated grips, connecting the stackable modules and completing the final plug-and-play connection. Sánchez emphasized that the system can be installed in less than ten minutes. As a benchmark, during the seventh FusionSolar Installer Summit, held in China with 48 teams from 36 countries, the average installation time was under five minutes, while the winning team completed the assembly in just 2 minutes and 32 seconds.
Commissioning is carried out through automatic connectivity via Huawei Home Gateway, NearLink communication and dual-channel WLAN, supported by a guided five-step setup process. To simplify distribution, five stock-keeping units (SKUs) cover the various LUTERRA S2 configurations.
The system provides power outputs of up to 10 kW in single-phase configurations and 20 kW in three-phase configurations. With the new Mini Backup Box, Huawei offers backup solutions of up to 60 kW, with a switchover time of 10 milliseconds.
Sánchez also explained that the system supports up to three inverters operating in parallel and up to 48 battery modules, providing a combined capacity of 336 kWh.
“It also supports integration with third-party inverters in existing photovoltaic installations, enables both grid-connected and off-grid operation, and provides monitoring of those inverters,” he said.
With LUTERRA S2, Huawei brings together energy storage, power conversion, backup capabilities and intelligent energy management on a single platform. The new residential solution combines simplified installation and commissioning with advanced safety features, flexible configuration options and integration with FusionSolar.
More information is available at

政策分类依据: 瑞士修订能源促进条例，提高光伏一次性投资补贴标准，属于可再生能源投资补助政策机制
content:
Markets & Policy
Switzerland has increased one-time payments for PV systems below 100 kW by CHF 40 ($47.99)/kW and raised the rate for installations below 150 kW that do not consume their own electricity.
Ralph Diermann
26 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Switzerland has increased its incentives for solar installations. The Federal Council has amended the Energy Promotion Ordinance (EnFV), raising one-time payments for PV systems in the below-30 kW and 30 kW to below-100 kW categories by CHF 40/kW. The power-based contribution is capped at 30% of the investment costs of reference systems. Building-integrated PV systems qualify for an additional payment of about 10%.
The Federal Council has also increased the rate for the high one-time payment (HEIV) for systems below 150 kW that do not consume their own electricity. The rate is now CHF 550/kW, with the power-based contribution capped at 60% of the investment costs of reference systems. Building-integrated systems do not qualify for an additional payment under this scheme. Industry association Swissolar says the increase will provide further incentives for solar deployment on apartment buildings, commercial properties and agricultural buildings, which have so far been underutilized.
Swissolar welcomed some aspects of the Federal Council’s decisions but criticized the omission of other measures it considers important for the solar industry. These include substantially simplifying price regulation for collective self-consumption schemes (ZEV) while maintaining tenant protections, fully using the statutory scope for reductions in grid charges for local electricity communities (LEG), and requiring default electricity suppliers to offer dynamic energy and grid tariffs as optional rates.
Swissolar also said that metering charges still lack upper limits and vary considerably between network operators. The association criticized the Federal Council for not increasing the cap on support for strengthening grid connection lines from CHF 50/kW to CHF 100/kW. It considers the current amount insufficient, particularly for agricultural installations.
ory changes
The Federal Council has also revised several other energy-related ordinances. Amendments to the Energy Ordinance (EnV) establish the required financial security for electricity storage projects under the Electricity Supply Act when the corresponding compensatory measure cannot be ordered at the same time as the construction project. The security must amount to at least 1.5 times the estimated cost of the compensatory measures.
The government has also abolished individually calculated fees for establishing collective self-consumption schemes (ZEV) and local electricity communities (LEG). The change standardizes the rules across Switzerland and is intended to simplify implementation of these models, which are important for solar deployment.
Through revisions to the Ordinance on the Planning Approval Procedure for Electrical Installations (VPeA), the Federal Council is also implementing a previously approved amendment to the Electricity Act (EleG). The planning process for transmission lines (SÜL) will be simplified. The Federal Council will no longer designate a planning area, but will instead directly determine the planning corridor and transmission technology, either overhead lines or underground cables. The changes are intended to simplify procedures and accelerate grid expansion.
The Federal Council has also revised the CO2 Ordinance (CO2-VO) following changes to the design of building-sector support programs. In future, only projects involving the direct use of geothermal energy will receive support. Costs already covered by third parties, such as cantons, will be excluded when calculating federal contributions, in line with the approach under the Energy Promotion Ordinance. Support for solar thermal systems used to provide process heat will also be discontinued.
The revisions also clarify CO2 emissions requirements for new vehicles. Among other changes, off-road vehicles will be excluded from the scope of the rules for heavy vehicles, in line with the EU approach. The baseline values used to calculate emissions targets will also be updated.

title: New 6-nm niobium phosphide wires could replace copper in future chips
content: Researchers at Stanford University have demonstrated an unusual electrical conductor that becomes more efficient as its wires get narrower, potentially overcoming a major limitation of copper wiring in next-generation computer chips.The team tested nanoribbons made from niobium phosphide (NbP), a topological semimetal that conducts electricity differently from conventional metals. The researchers found that its electrical resistivity decreases as the ribbons become narrower, allowing the material to outperform similarly sized copper conductors at extremely small dimensions.The study could offer a new approach to building the nanoscale interconnects that connect billions of transistors and other components inside modern processors.Copper has long served as the primary wiring material in computer chips. However, as manufacturers shrink these connections to just a few nanometers, electrons increasingly scatter from wire surfaces and grain boundaries. This raises electrical resistance, wastes energy as heat and makes signal transmission less efficient.The problem becomes particularly important in high-density chips, where billions of connections must operate within a small area.Semimetal reverses copper limitsTo investigate an alternative, the researchers fabricated flat niobium phosphide nanoribbons as narrow as 5 to 6 nanometers and approximately 1.5 nanometers thick.At a cross-sectional area of about 9 square nanometers, the nanoribbons achieved an electrical resistivity of 18 ± 4.1 micro-ohm centimetres at room temperature. The researchers reported that this was lower than that of conventional metals and semimetals with comparable dimensions.Unlike copper, where most electrical current travels through the material’s core, niobium phosphide can carry a greater proportion of current along its surfaces and edges.This behaviour is linked to its topological properties, particularly spin-momentum locking, which reduces electron backscattering. As the nanoribbons become narrower, surface and edge conduction contribute more significantly to the overall current.The team also found that this conduction remained relatively insensitive to manufacturing imperfections, including surface roughness and oxidation.Eric Pop, a professor of electrical engineering at Stanford and senior author of the study, compared the problem with water flowing through pipes. A wide pipe carries water efficiently, but narrowing it to the size of a straw makes its walls increasingly restrictive. Similarly, surface scattering makes copper less efficient as its dimensions shrink.Niobium phosphide, by contrast, allows electrons to travel more efficiently along its surfaces at these extremely small scales.Chip manufacturing potentialThe researchers said the material’s performance at room temperature and compatibility with industry-standard fabrication techniques make it promising for future semiconductor manufacturing.The team used top-down nanofabrication methods to pattern the material into narrow ribbons, rather than relying on a specialized manufacturing approach designed exclusively for laboratory demonstrations.However, the material is not yet ready to replace copper in commercial processors. Researchers still need to investigate its long-term endurance, fabrication compatibility, and behavior across different operating temperatures.The team is also examining other semimetals that could offer similar or better electrical performance.The work involved researchers from Stanford University, SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, Pennsylvania State University, the Weizmann Institute of Science and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company.The findings suggest that topological semimetals could provide an alternative route to reducing resistance in increasingly compact chip interconnects, where conventional copper wiring faces growing physical limitations.The study was published in the journal Nature.
