title: China's 1,300-mph J-20 stealth jet joins forces with combat drones
content: China is incorporating artificial intelligence and autonomous drone support into routine fighter pilot training, giving its aircrews experience with combat scenarios involving multiple aircraft. The approach pairs conventional fighter operations with unmanned wingmen, allowing pilots to practice coordinated missions inside advanced flight simulators.The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) has begun integrating manned-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) exercises into training systems used by frontline aviation units. The simulations also introduce complex battlefield conditions designed to test how pilots respond to increasingly demanding combat situations.Simulating drone-assisted combatA report from the PLA Daily revealed that an aviation brigade under the Southern Theatre Command has incorporated MUM-T exercises into its ground-based flight simulators. The training targets younger pilots and introduces them to operations involving autonomous supporting aircraft.Pilots can practice extended combat engagements with simulated adversaries while receiving assistance from unmanned loyal wingman drones. The system also generates changing battlefield conditions, including successive groups of approaching targets and electromagnetic interference.These scenarios expose pilots to challenges beyond conventional air-to-air engagements. Electronic interference can complicate communications and sensor operations, forcing pilots to adapt their decisions during simulated missions.The report did not identify the fighter aircraft involved in these exercises. However, its accompanying photograph showed a Shenyang J-16 assigned to the unnamed aviation brigade.The training approach also builds on earlier simulator exercises involving geographically separated participants. A December 2025 PLA Daily report described a Central Theatre Command pilot conducting simulated engagements alongside personnel operating real military equipment thousands of kilometers away.The exercise combined system-generated loyal wingman drones with live participants. It offered a way to recreate coordinated combat scenarios without requiring every participating aircraft to fly together.J-20 enters the equationChina’s experiments with MUM-T extend beyond simulator training. Research published in June by the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI) traced the PLA Air Force’s combat method validation efforts to 2024.The study identified the Ninth Aviation Brigade as a participant in developing coordinated penetration tactics for the Chengdu J-20 stealth fighter. These operations involve manned and unmanned aircraft working together during missions.Based at Wuhu airbase in Anhui province, the brigade operates within the Eastern Theatre Command. It also ranks among the earliest PLA Air Force units to receive the fifth-generation J-20.China offered a public glimpse of these capabilities in November 2025. A promotional video marking the PLA Air Force’s 76th anniversary showed a Gongji-11 (GJ-11) stealth combat drone flying alongside a J-20.The footage also featured a J-16D electronic warfare aircraft. The GJ-11, identified by the codename Xuanlong 08, demonstrated China’s interest in coordinating different aircraft through shared missions.Autonomous wingmen take shapeChinese state broadcaster CCTV aired additional footage earlier in November 2026. It showed the GJ-11 operating alongside a J-16 and separately alongside J-20 fighters.The footage offers further evidence of China’s efforts to integrate unmanned aircraft into conventional air combat operations. title: XPENG unveils humanoid robot with 1,500 tactile sensors in China
content: XPENG has unveiled a new physical-intelligence architecture and its IRON humanoid robot, outlining plans to bring the machine into its retail stores in 2027 as the Chinese automaker expands into robotics and autonomous mobility.The company introduced its Turing Physical AI Architecture, also called VLA 3.0, at its eighth AI Day in Guangzhou on November 25. The framework connects AI models with computing, perception, control systems, and physical hardware across intelligent vehicles and humanoid robots.XPENG said the architecture has three systems operating at different speeds. System 0 coordinates hardware functions, including power, energy, communication, and execution, while feeding information about the body’s state back into the AI loop.System 1, powered by the company’s VLA 2.0 model, interprets the surrounding environment and translates it into real-time actions. System 2 handles higher-level cognition, using vision-language task planning and an agent runtime system to interpret objectives and coordinate complex tasks.The company said the three layers create a feedback loop in which physical actions inform subsequent decisions. Its latest VLA 2.0 model, version 6.4.0, supports agent-driven closed-loop training, which XPENG said increases training speed by 10 to 12 times.IRON targets retail rolesIRON, which made its first public appearance at the event, has 76 degrees of freedom and more than 1,500 tactile sensing points. XPENG said sensors cover more than 80 percent of key body areas, while three proprietary Turing AI chips support onboard models and whole-body control.The robot combines multimodal understanding and task planning with navigation, manipulation, and safety monitoring. It can navigate autonomously, receive tasks through voice or app instructions, charge itself, and report abnormal conditions, according to the company.XPENG plans to begin training IRON as a store assistant in its retail outlets in the first quarter of 2027. Its official public release is targeted for the second quarter.The company has established a robot data factory covering more than 250 scenarios and 15 job categories. Its automated assembly line includes more than 600 holographic quality-inspection items and over 1,000 tests for complete robots and key components.Vehicles join robotics pushXPENG is extending its physical-intelligence strategy into vehicles. Its X-VMC 2.0 motion-control system connects propulsion, braking, steering and suspension, allowing software to coordinate driving, safety, comfort and energy management.A feature called VLA Adaptive Deceleration adjusts braking and energy recovery when a driver releases the accelerator. XPENG said tests in urban congestion showed a 12.4 percent increase in usable driving range compared with having energy recovery switched off. The feature is scheduled for its first over-the-air rollout in December 2026.The company said its robotaxi program moved from staffed to driverless road testing in eight months and obtained an L4 demonstration-operation qualification in Guangzhou. Driverless passenger tests have begun, with demonstration operations in selected areas planned by the end of 2026.XPENG’s first purpose-built robotaxi, the YOYO-01, is scheduled for release in 2027. Its ARIDGE business is advancing a manned electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft program towards airworthiness certification.XPENG aims to use a shared technology foundation across vehicles, robots, and flying vehicles, while adapting systems for different hardware and tasks.

title: Neuralink gets FDA approval for first pivotal brain implant trial
content: Neuralink has received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal clinical trial in the country for an implantable brain-computer interface (BCI). The study will evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the company’s technology in people with severe paralysis caused by amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).Announcing the development on November 25, Neuralink said the trial builds on its ongoing early feasibility studies in the US, Canada and the UK, which have involved more than 30 implanted participants. Together, these participants have contributed thousands of hours of real-world use of the company’s brain-computer interface.The LINK Pivotal Study will examine how effectively participants can use the Neuralink system to control digital devices through thought. The company said the research would focus on functional outcomes that could improve independence in everyday life, alongside the long-term safety and reliability of the implant.Neuralink said enrolment for the study is now open, with the programme expected to expand across multiple clinical sites in the US.Implant reads brain signalsThe system being evaluated uses Neuralink’s N1 Implant, which records neural activity through fine electrode threads placed in the brain’s motor cortex, the region associated with movement.The implant detects electrical signals associated with intended movements and translates them into commands that allow users to interact with digital devices. Participants can learn to move a computer cursor by imagining moving their hand, without physically moving their limbs.Neuralink’s existing Telepathy programme has demonstrated cursor navigation and mouse functions, including left, right and middle clicks. Participants have also used the technology for activities such as messaging, browsing the internet, writing code, creating digital artwork and playing video games.The implant is inserted using the company’s R1 surgical robot, which places the fine electrode threads into the brain. The N1 device sits within the skull, with no external wires or battery pack. It communicates wirelessly with a computer and can also be charged wirelessly through the scalp.Neuralink’s clinical-trial information says participants undergo surgery under general anaesthesia. The company’s published study pathway includes health screening, brain imaging, implantation, device training and follow-up assessments.Pivotal trial marks milestoneThe new study represents a move beyond Neuralink’s earlier-stage human testing. Its PRIME programme was designed as an early feasibility study to evaluate the initial safety and functionality of the N1 Implant, R1 Robot and associated software in people with paralysis.A pivotal trial is a later-stage clinical investigation intended to generate evidence about a medical device’s safety and effectiveness for a specific intended use. Such evidence can support a subsequent regulatory application, although successful completion does not guarantee marketing authorisation.Importantly, the FDA’s approval to launch LINK does not mean the Neuralink implant has been approved for general medical use. The company continues to describe its devices as investigational and available only through authorised clinical research.Neuralink’s trial information identifies adults living with ALS as eligible for the pivotal study. Its published participation pathway also outlines follow-up assessments extending to 24 months after implantation, allowing researchers to monitor device performance and participant safety over time.The company’s announcement did not disclose the planned number of participants or provide a detailed breakdown of clinical sites.The milestone could bring Neuralink closer to establishing the clinical evidence needed for a future regulatory submission. However, the pivotal study will need to demonstrate that the implant can provide reliable digital-device control while maintaining an acceptable safety profile over an extended period.

title: SpaceX gets FCC approval for one million space data center satellites
content: SpaceX has received federal approval to pursue one of the largest satellite infrastructure projects ever proposed. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has authorized Elon Musk’s company to deploy up to 1 million satellites under its Starmind orbital computing initiative. The network would move substantial computing workloads beyond Earth’s atmosphere as demand for advanced computing infrastructure continues to grow.The authorization marks the first time the FCC has approved an entire constellation dedicated to space-based data centers. SpaceX wants to distribute computing hardware across orbit and use the resulting processing capacity to support applications on Earth.How Starmind will process dataStarmind would operate as an interconnected network of orbital computing modules. Each satellite would process information in space before transmitting results back to Earth. The architecture would shift some computing workloads away from conventional terrestrial data centers.SpaceX plans to connect the satellites through optical inter-satellite links. These laser-based connections would allow spacecraft to exchange information without depending entirely on ground stations. Radiofrequency communications would provide additional connectivity when necessary.The FCC has also authorized backup radio links for telemetry, tracking, and command operations. These connections would help SpaceX monitor its satellites and maintain control during emergencies. The approval covers the 18.8–19.3 GHz downlink and 28.6–29.1 GHz uplink frequency bands.Moving computing infrastructure into orbit could address several limitations facing terrestrial data centers. Large facilities require substantial electricity and sophisticated cooling infrastructure to handle demanding computing workloads. SpaceX argues that orbital facilities could harness solar energy more efficiently while reducing some of these requirements.However, operating powerful computers in space introduces significant engineering challenges. Electronic hardware generates considerable heat during intensive processing. Satellites must dissipate that heat without conventional air-based cooling systems.SpaceX must also demonstrate that it can manufacture, launch, and maintain such an enormous satellite network. The company’s developing Starship rocket could play an important role in making deployment economically viable.Massive deployment challengeThe FCC’s authorization does not mean SpaceX can immediately deploy its entire proposed constellation. The company must meet several deployment milestones over the coming years.SpaceX must place its first operational satellite in orbit by November 2033. The authorization requires 100,000 operational satellites by November 2035. The company must reach half its approved constellation by November 2038.Full deployment must follow by November 2040. Even with regulatory approval, achieving those targets will require substantial advances in launch capacity and satellite manufacturing.The FCC also left certain aspects of SpaceX’s proposal unresolved. The company must address additional regulatory requirements concerning satellite disposal. The agency will continue reviewing other orbital data center proposals through its established procedures.SpaceX also announced Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued Class A common share to every active Trump Account. These tax-advantaged investment accounts help American children build long-term savings.SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary. We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans. Today, we are committing one SpaceX share to millions of American children…— SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 25, 2026Musk will personally match the number of shares contributed by SpaceX. The commitment fulfills a pledge he made on X in October 2026 to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States. At the time, the proposed contribution covered approximately 73 million children and carried an estimated value of $10.7 billion.SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell separately announced a personal contribution exceeding 2 million company shares. The commitments extend the company’s ownership initiative to younger Americans as it pursues its ambitious plans across space transportation and orbital computing.

title: Anthropic CEO rejects giving machines control over human governance
content: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has rejected suggestions that humanity should surrender its political authority to artificial intelligence. He argues that increasingly capable AI systems can transform society without replacing democratic institutions or human decision-making. His clarification follows a November 25 Axios report examining disagreements among technology leaders over humanity’s future relationship with superintelligent machines.Amodei addressed the controversy in a lengthy post on X. He said his public writing has consistently supported democratic oversight of AI. Critics, he argued, have confused his support for automating complex tasks with advocating machine-led governance.Democracy remains the boundaryAmodei compared arguments for AI-led governance with historical defenses of autocracy. Advocates have long argued that centralized authority enables faster decisions than democratic institutions. However, he believes efficiency cannot justify sacrificing political legitimacy or people’s right to determine their future.No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going… https://t.co/DUQxWZDPAk— Dario Amodei (@DarioAmodei) November 25, 2026His 2024 essay, Machines of Loving Grace, explored how advanced AI could strengthen democratic participation. He proposed using AI to help citizens understand public policy, resolve disagreements, and identify common ground. The objective was to improve democratic decision-making, not transfer political authority to machines.He revisited these concerns in The Adolescence of Technology, published in January 2026. The essay examined how powerful AI could enable authoritarian governments and threaten individual freedoms. Amodei also warned against technology companies accumulating excessive political power. His latest clarification extends that argument to companies attempting to hand authority to AI itself.Automation creates difficult tradeoffsAmodei’s position becomes more nuanced when discussing individual tasks. He supports AI handling increasingly complex work across medicine, transportation, software development, and energy. Such applications could accelerate research, improve productivity, and save lives.However, he sees several reasons to restrict certain deployments. One concern involves recursive self-improvement, where AI systems help develop increasingly capable successors. In his September 2026 essay, We Must Pace the Frontier, Amodei warned that this process could outpace researchers’ ability to understand and control AI development.Anthropic also does not consider it safe for Claude to develop successive frontier models entirely autonomously without meaningful human supervision. Amodei believes safety research must keep pace with improvements in AI capabilities.Employment presents another challenge. End-to-end automation could disrupt jobs faster than workers can adapt. Some deployments might therefore require delays. He also cautioned against blindly trusting AI-generated alignment research.AI leaders face accountability questionsAmodei also criticized technology executives who promote slogans about human agency and control. He questioned whether those commitments translate into meaningful differences in their products and deployment decisions.He defended Anthropic’s refusal to let its models power fully autonomous weapons, despite potential legal consequences in its dispute with the US government. He presented that decision as evidence that the company’s stated principles carry practical consequences.Amodei believes decisions about automation should involve governments, democratic institutions, AI developers, and individual consumers. No single authority should make every decision.His central argument separates technological capability from political legitimacy. AI may eventually perform increasingly complex work, but that does not give machines the right to decide humanity’s future.

title: US-made solid-state batteries could pack more energy without pressure

政策分类依据: NYSERDA向储能技术研发项目提供竞争性研究拨款支持
content: A new type of solid-state batteries which could store more energy and withstand repeated charging cycles without external pressure, has just received substantial financial backing by the US. The batteries are being developed by New York’s InfinitEnergy, an energy storage startup co-founded by Quinn Qiao, PhD, chair of the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at Syracuse University, and Anthony Terrinoni, a staff member at the department.The firm recently secured USD 250,000 from the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA). The funds will support the development of the cells and address their reliance on external mechanical pressure to operate reliably. As per the university, the funding is part of a nearly USD 13 million investment in 15 energy storage projects. Their goal is to strengthen the state’s power grid and reduce its dependence on fossil fuels. New battery designSolid-state batteries use solid electrolytes, rather than a liquid or gel, to conduct the ions between the anode and cathode. The electrolyte also acts as a physical barrier to prevent short circuits. The solid-state electrolytes usually have greater chemical and thermal stability than liquid ones. At the same time, solid electrolytes can also enable batteries to achieve higher energy densities. Some solid-state battery designs could reach 500 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg), compared to roughly 250 Wh/kg in conventional lithium-ion (Li-ion) cells.Quinn Qiao talking to students in the lab.Credit: Alex DunbarHowever several technical challenges have prevented solid-state cells’ widespread adoption, including the need for external mechanical pressure to keep the contact between the different components inside the cells. The extra equipment needed to maintain this pressure can make batteries harder to build, heavier and bulkier.To tackle this challenge, the team aims to develop solid-state batteries that can operate without external pressure. The final goal is to make this happen without compromising energy density or cycle life. “Removing the need for external mechanical pressure while keeping high energy density and long cycle life is one of the biggest barriers to practical deployment, and this support lets us move that work from the lab toward real-world use,” Qiao said. “We’re grateful to NYSERDA, and proud that this effort is rooted in Syracuse and New York.”Nearing commercial useThe firm has not yet disclosed the chemical composition of the cells, their energy density, or the number of charging and discharging cycles they could withstand. They are certain, however, that their approach could ultimately lead to safer and commercially viable energy storage solutions. The project was funded via NYSERDA’s Power Generation and Storage Innovation program. The program supports the development and demonstration of energy storage technologies that are not yet commercially available.According to Terrinoni, the funding brings the company closer to commercializing the technology. “This NYSERDA award is an important milestone for InfinitEnergy as we advance our next-generation solid-state battery technology,” Terrinoni said. “This investment brings us one step closer to transforming innovative energy storage solutions into real-world products.”Doreen M. Harris, NYSERDA CEO and president, explained that advanced energy storage technologies are essential to strengthening New York’s power grid and making the most of its energy resources. “These projects will advance promising solutions that can deliver power when it is needed most,” Harris concluded in a press release.

title: Germany tests hydrogen fuel cell tractor with 500-bar mobile station
content: Researchers in Germany have invented a hydrogen fuel cell tractor equipped with 350-bar tanks, and are currently testing whether it can replace diesel tractors and reduce emissions from farming.Dubbed H2tofielddrive, the project is carried out by scientists at the University of Bonn. Its goal is to evaluate one of Germany’s first hydrogen fuel cell tractors and determine whether it could be used in everyday farming.To overcome the refueling challenges, the team also acquired a mobile hydrogen station that operates at a pressure of 500 bar. The station supplies hydrogen to the university’s research farm without the need for fixed refueling facilities.Jürgen Rath, PhD, a researcher from the University of Bonn said that the team will now assess the tractor’s energy efficiency and performance, and examine what is needed to use hydrogen-powered machinery. “The energy efficiency of hydrogen compared to conventional fossil fuels in agricultural tractors is being investigated as part of a doctoral research project at the University of Bonn,” he added. Running on hydrogenAccording to the team, refueling the tractor posed a massive challenge at first. Its hydrogen tanks operate at aa pressure of 350 bar (5,076 pounds per square inch). So, to refuel it without an additional compressor, they needed a hydrogen supply at a higher pressure. To tackle the matter, energy supplier Knauber secured access to hydrogen at the required pressure through its network and took responsibility for the logistics of the hydrogen supply. The mobile station acquired by the university operates at 500 bar (7,252 pounds per square inch).Refueling the hydrogen fuel cell tractor with the mobile hydrogen station.Credit: Campus Klein-Altendorf / Uni BonnRath explained that the trailer-like mobile station brings hydrogen directly to the testing site at the university’s Klein-Altendorf campus. The tractor can, hence, be refueled without a permanent refueling station. However, mobile refueling solutions remain relatively scarce in the country, which their implementation a technical and logistical challenge. “The development of a hydrogen economy requires not only innovative applications but also the right infrastructure,” Mortiz Kroymann, Knauber sales manager, said. “Projects like this provide important insights into the future use of hydrogen in agriculture.”A cleaner alternativeThe initiative is being carried out at the university’s Chair of Renewable Resources as part of an interdisciplinary doctoral study. The team pointed out that hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity through a reaction between hydrogen and oxygen. The process produces water and heat and does not release carbon dioxide (CO2). However, the fuel’s environmental footprint depends on how it is produced and delivered. The researchers will now collect empirical data on the tractor’s energy efficiency and performance and compare its efficiency with that of conventional fossil fuel-powered tractors.The hydrogen-powered tractor alongside conventional agricultural machinery.Credit: Campus Klein-Altendorf / Uni BonnAt the same time, they will test several practical aspects of hydrogen adoption in agriculture, among which infrastructure, fuel supply logistics, regulatory permits, and everyday operating procedures.“In this context, it was important for us to find a regional partner who could not only supply hydrogen but also understand the project’s specific requirements,” Rath concluded in a press statement. “This is an important factor in the project’s continued progress.”

Dutch government opens tender for 2GW IJmuiden Ver Gamma offshore wind sites TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Dutch government opens tender for 2GW IJmuiden Ver Gamma offshore wind sites
The tender for the IJmuiden
Ver Gamma-A
and Gamma-B
offshore wind sites opened on 26 November 2026 and is due to close on 10
December 2026.
The two Dutch offshore wind projects, which together have a planned capacity
of 2 GW, are being tendered simultaneously, with the maximum tender amount
set at €117/MWh for Gamma-A and €116/MWh for Gamma-B.
According to the announcement, once bids have been assessed, subsidy applications
will follow. The maximum subsidy budget has been set at €4.758 billion
for Gamma-A and €4.698 billion for Gamma-B.
The projects mark another milestone in the Netherlands' energy transition,
helping to expand domestic renewable energy generation and reduce reliance
on imported energy.
Transmission system operator TenneT has been selected to develop the offshore
grid infrastructure required to meet the country's offshore wind targets.
The wind farms will be connected to a TenneT offshore converter platform
featuring a 2 GW direct current (DC) connection to an onshore substation.
The two sites form part of the IJmuiden Ver Wind Farm Zone (IJVWFZ), which
comprises four sites including, Alpha, Beta, Gamma-A and Gamma-B. Together,
the four sites are expected to deliver around 6 GW of installed offshore
wind capacity.

title: Lowestoft Port chosen to support the 2.8GW Vanguard projects
content:
During a visit by Energy Minister Michael Shanks to the Port of Lowestoft's
Eastern Energy Facility (LEEF), RWE, in partnership with Associated British
Ports (ABP) and Clarkson's Port Services (CPS), announced plans to establish
facilities at the port to support the 2.8 GW Norfolk Vanguard West and
East offshore wind projects.
According to the announcement, RWE is working with ABP and CPS to finalise
agreements for the port to serve as the long-term operations and maintenance
base for the projects.
"Britain's clean energy future is being built in towns like Lowestoft,
drawing on generations of industrial expertise and creating opportunities
for the next generation," Energy Minister Michael Shanks said.
RWE said the projects are expected to support and create around 2,800 jobs
across the supply chain during the three-year construction period, with
a further 300 jobs once the wind farms become operational.
Tom Glover, UK country chair at RWE, said: "The £12 billion investment
in the Vanguard West and East offshore wind farms represents a major commitment
to the UK's clean energy future, and we're delighted that Lowestoft will
play a vital role in turning that investment into reality."

title: ITRI and ORE Catapult extend offshore wind partnership
content:
The Industrial Technology Research Institute(ITRI) and
the Offshore Renewable Energy (ORE) Catapult have renewed their green energy
partnership through 2031, building on five years of collaboration in offshore
wind innovation.
The extended agreement will focus on floating offshore wind, operations
and maintenance (O&M), data quality, artificial intelligence and digital
technologies.
The partnership also supports Taiwan's ambition to strengthen its position
as an Asia Pacific hub for these technologies while contributing to regional
net-zero goals.According to ITRI, Taiwan's offshore wind sector is entering
a new phase were improving O&M efficiency and reducing costs have become
key priorities.
“These tools enable operators to closely monitor meteorological conditions
and turbine health, minimise unnecessary vessel dispatches and manual inspections,
and ensure more reliable offshore operations, even in the Taiwan Strait’s
harsh marine environment,”said Pei-Fang
Liang, Deputy General Director of ITRI’s Green Energy and Environment
Research Laboratories.
ORE Catapult said the renewed partnership will combine the UK's offshore
wind expertise with ITRI's experience in Taiwan to expand collaboration
across the Asia Pacific region. Areas of focus include Japan, South Korea,
Australia, the Philippines and Vietnam, with an emphasis on addressing
deepwater offshore wind challenges and supporting floating wind development.
The partners will continue their collaboration through joint task forces,
technical exchanges and research initiatives aimed at advancing offshore
wind innovation and sustainability.

title: Entrion Wind secures offshore demonstration project for fondation technology
content:
Fondation OPEN-C has awarded Entrion Wind a demonstration project for its
patented Fully Restrained Platform (FRP) monopile foundation technology
at the SEM-REV offshore test site in France's Pays de la Loire region.
The project was awarded through the OPEN SEA demonstration call for expressions
of interest and follows a joint application with SEALENCE, a cleantech
company specialising in underwater noise mitigation solutions.
Entrion Wind said its FRP monopile technology could extend the economic
viability of fixed-bottom offshore wind projects into deeper waters by
combining a monopile foundation with pretensioned mooring lines and a Top
Mooring Assembly (TMA).
The demonstration project will evaluate the FRP's performance in a real
offshore environment, including foundation fabrication, installation, operations
and maintenance methods. The testing programme is expected to support the
technology's progression to Technology Readiness Level 8 (TRL 8).
"We believe FRP has the potential to significantly expand the range
of offshore sites where fixed-bottom wind can remain economically competitive,"
said Eivind Johnsen, CEO of Entrion Wind.
SEALENCE is also expected to test its SubSea Quieter Noise Abatement Solution,
adapted for use with Entrion Wind's foundation technology.
"Entrion Wind's project fully illustrates our ambition to make offshore
testing a driver of competitiveness for the offshore wind industry while
creating new opportunities for the local industrial ecosystem," said
Stéven Curet, managing director of Fondation OPEN-C.

content:
Prysmian has received a notice to proceed for seven projects that will
connect the Dodecanese and North Aegean islands to the Greek national grid.
The notice was awarded by the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO).
Under the framework agreement signed in June, the projects are worth up
Prysmian will design, manufacture and install 900km of high-voltage alternating
current (HVAC) cables for both onshore and offshore connections. Installation
is expected to reach water depths of more than 1,150 metres.
According to the company, the interconnectors will reduce the islands'
reliance on diesel and oil-fired power generation by making it easier to
integrate solar and wind energy and distribute electricity across the country.
Final delivery of the projects is currently expected in 2033.
Raul Gil, EVP Transmission at Prysmian, said: “These interconnectors will
make a real difference to daily life on the islands. Residents, local businesses
and visitors will benefit from a more reliable electricity supply.
“We expect to set a new world record for HVAC cable installation, and
we can take on that challenge because we have the cable technology, the
installation vessels and the expertise needed to deliver it successfully.”

title: S&P Discovers Nvidia’s Governance Lapses
content: Credit agencies aren’t known for being ahead of the pack when it comes to spotting weaknesses at companies. (If you don’t believe me, check out their role in the 2008 financial crisis .) But S&P’s note on Wednesday , alerting the market to the possibility it could downgrade Nvidia’s credit rating, sets new standards in stating the obvious. S&P declared that the recent drama surrounding CEO Jensen Huang “exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia’s management and governance framework.” That’s true, but some of the vulnerabilities it cited, around “board structure, composition and effectiveness,” were hiding in plain sight. For instance, Nvidia’s board didn’t have a chairperson until two weeks ago, when Huang resigned and Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia’s “first-ever chair.” (Huang was reinstated on Monday.) Nvidia explained in past securities filings that its board “ensures that each member has an equal voice in the affairs and management of NVIDIA by having an independent Lead Director, rather than a chairperson.” Some might say going without a chair empowered Huang—it’s a governance weakness that S&P could have flagged in the past.

title: How Bankers Are Turning Tech Stock Volatility Into Cash
content: Tech firms spending heavily on AI buildouts have flooded the market with new stock sales this year. And with investments in AI infrastructure soaking up so much investor cash, raising money for other capital-hungry areas of tech like quantum computing and robotics is requiring especially creative dealmaking. For companies that are already public but need more cash for ambitious projects, sharp swings in their share prices are making it tough to sell more stock at an attractive price. Bankers say one workaround is turning that volatility into a selling point by bundling shares with warrants, which give investors the right to buy more stock later at a locked-in price. If investors are willing to pay up for a chance at a future payoff, companies can sell stock at a premium rather than the usual discount for new share sales. One recent example is quantum computing company IonQ, which raised $2 billion in mid-October at a 15% premium to its prior closing price. In the IonQ deal, investors got stock plus warrants to buy more shares at double the stock’s pre-offering price within the next seven years, an extra way for them to profit if IonQ’s stock soars. IonQ has raised $5 billion in total through three such offerings since July 2025, helping pay for an acquisition spree that expanded its business into chip manufacturing and cybersecurity. The company’s stock has been volatile over that period, falling sharply from an October 2025 high of $82, rebounding to about $70 this May and then tumbling again. The shares currently trade around $21. With tech investors particularly skittish right now, there’s more reason for cash-hungry companies to pounce on any opportunities to raise money. That’s also boosting the appeal of at-the-market stock sales, which allow companies to sell shares gradually into the open market, giving them the flexibility to take advantage of rallies. And while less conventional ways of raising equity were once viewed on Wall Street as signs of desperation, bankers say that stigma has faded in recent years as companies have embraced the benefits of having more options for raising cash. “Historically, ATMs and some of these more creative financing tools have been a bit of a scarlet letter...it was hard to get a management team or board around them,” said Connor Leahey, managing director at Cohen & Co. Capital Markets. “And now it's totally shifted.” But getting to the public market in the first place has also become much tougher. Investors have had to sop up a surge in new stock issued by already-public tech giants this year alongside mega listings from SpaceX and last week’s debut by Anthropic, with most of those shares performing poorly after their IPOs. The broader market for tech debuts has all but dried up, and Anthropic’s rapid drop below its offering price doesn’t bode well for other IPO hopefuls. That helps explain a comparative burst of activity in mergers with special purpose acquisition companies. Five companies went public via a SPAC merger in October, including two space technology firms and a semiconductor tech company, according to data and analytics company Boardroom Alpha . Four more companies have gone public via SPAC so far this month, including robotics company Agility Robotics and spacecraft developer Quantum Space. Public debuts via SPAC boomed in 2020 and 2021 before falling sharply in recent years after a string of poorly performing deals and other market headwinds. But companies and bankers are taking a renewed look at SPACs as an IPO alternative. In a SPAC deal, a cash-poor private tech firm is acquired by a cashed-up public shell of a company. (SPAC stands for special purpose acquisition company). “SPACs are still alive,” said Steven Halperin, co-head of capital solutions and head of public equity markets at Moelis & Co. “And as the IPO market gets more fickle and transaction sizes become larger and larger, will more companies think about going this route?” One reason why the SPAC route may be more appealing right now is a proposed regulatory change that could make it easier for newly public companies to raise new equity after their debut. One drawback of SPACs is that they don’t guarantee a big infusion of cash, since investors in the SPAC can typically cash out their shares before the merger closes, which they often do if they don’t like the business getting acquired. The Securities and Exchange Commission in May proposed easing restrictions on stock sales by newly public companies, including ones that go public via a SPAC. Among other changes, the proposal would eliminate a one-year waiting period for newly public companies to register for fast-tracked stock offerings. That could make it easier for those companies to take advantage of rallies in their share prices, including through ATMs and other deals already gaining traction with their public peers. title: The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
content:
The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel
Avi Davidson is the first at-home user of an experimental prosthetic hand that lets him feel his wife’s hand in his own.
Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.
Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.
The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.
Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb
In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.
The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.
Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”
Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.
The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections
A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.
Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.
A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”
In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.
Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.
The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.
To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”
The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic
Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.
He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.
At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”
Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.
The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.
Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.
The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.
The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.
Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”
Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

title: Intelligente Einlegesohle misst Druckbelastungen mit gedruckten Sensoren
content:
Intelligente Einlegesohle misst Druckbelastungen mit gedruckten Sensoren
Vielversprechende Forschungsergebnisse: Smarte Technologie erkennt kritische Belastungen am Fuß für Menschen mit diabetischem Fußsyndrom
Stell Dir vor, Schuhsohlen besitzen in Zukunft ein Gehirn: Sensorische Einlagen überwachen das Gangbild, melden ungünstige Druckverhältnisse in Echtzeit ans Handy. Sogar den Blutzuckerspiegel misst die Sohle dabei indirekt. Eine KI-gestützte Analyse reagiert, bevor etwas Schlimmes passiert. Science Fiction? Im Rahmen des Teilprojektes aus dem Forschungsprojekt „GLUCOSole“ entwickeln Prof. Dr. Denys Matthies und Marco Gabrecht, Promovend am Promotionskolleg SH, dieses Werkzeug, das besonders Menschen mit Diabetes unterstützen kann: Individuell gefertigte Schuhsohlen mit Sensoren erfassen Bewegungs- und Druckdaten und ermöglichen mit Unterstützung von KI eine effektive Gesundheitsüberwachung.
Austausch wichtig für Weiterentwicklung in der Forschung
„Unser Prototyp hat sehr viel Potential für die Anwendung“, so Marco Gabrecht. Diabetische Fußprobleme zählen zu den häufigsten Komplikationen bei Altersdiabetes mit gravierenden Folgen wie Schmerzen, Mobilitätsverlust und Amputationen. Gabrecht wird seine neuesten Forschungsergebnisse Anfang Dezember 2026 auf der Konferenz ACM SCF 2026 in Japan vorstellen und sich dort intensiv mit anderen Forschenden austauschen. „Ohne Austausch; keine Weiterentwicklung“, sagt er. „Auch in unserer Fachgruppe Cyber-Physical & Human Systems wird immer wieder über den Tellerrand geschaut: Wie kann Technik den Menschen mit KI unterstützen?“
Menschen mit Diabetes haben häufig Probleme an den Füßen
Schon in seiner Masterarbeit hat sich Gabrecht mit Schuhsohlen beschäftigt. „Schuhe hat man immer dabei. Die vergisst man nicht. Wenn die uns intelligent unterstützen können, wäre das eine gute Idee.“ Schon mal auf einen spitzen Stein getreten und blitzschnell das Gewicht verlagert? Was bei gesunden Menschen das Nervensystem misst, das Gehirn verrechnet und als Handlungsimpuls an die Muskulatur zurücksendet, funktioniert bei Menschen mit Diabetes nicht gut. Betroffene spüren Schmerzen, Hitze, Kälte oder drohende Druckstellen kaum, haben dazu besonders häufig ein ungünstiges Gangmuster. Es kann passieren, dass sie den Fuß unbemerkt lange Zeit falsch belasten und die so entstehenden Druckstellen erst bemerken, wenn sie abends die Socken ausziehen. Die Wunden heilen zudem auch noch langsamer als bei gesunden Menschen aufgrund von Mikrozirkulationsstörungen.
Kombination von zwei Messprinzipien an jeweils sechs Druckpunkten
Die Wissenschaftler der Technischen Hochschule Lübeck haben als Antwort auf dieses Problem eine intelligente Einlegesohle entwickelt, die an sechs Messstellen Druckbelastungen unter dem Fuß mit zwei unterschiedlichen Messprinzipien erfasst. Neben ähnlichen Forschungsprojekten aus der Fachgruppe, wie SAFE und Mental Well, wird das Projekt GLUCOSole als Teil der GRANNI-Community in den Räumen des Fraunhofer IMTE durchgeführt, die sich für gesundes Altern und nachhaltige Medizintechnik einsetzt. „Die 3D-gedruckten Sensoren befinden sich unter der Großzehe, mehreren Mittelfußknochen, dem Mittelfuß und der Ferse, jeder misst die Druckverteilung sowohl kapazitiv als auch resistiv“, erläutert Gabrecht. Wie ist der Untergrund? Wie ist die Druckverteilung? Die Beschleunigung? Die Drehung? Wie rollt der Fuß ab? Ist die Position gut? Die Kombination zweier Messprinzipien soll künftig einen größeren Druckbereich abdecken als ein einzelner Sensortyp.
Schuhsohle an Handy: „Bitte Belastung verändern“
Die Signale werden über Bluetooth entweder ans Telefon oder an den Computer gesendet und ausgewertet. „Das Handy soll in Zukunft dann vibrieren und der Person melden, was nicht in Ordnung ist“, so Gabrecht. „Sie kann dann reagieren und eine Druckstelle vermeiden.“ Oder, noch weitergedacht: Sensoren messen, Aktoren führen aus: Die Sohle vibriert. Oder: Luft wird in der Sohle verschoben, sie wird so an einer Stelle dicker und gleicht ein Ungleichgewicht aus.
Die Möglichkeiten für die Praxis sind vielfältig. „In diesem Forschungsprojekte haben wir uns auf den konkreten Fall diabetischer Fuß fokussiert“, so Matthies. Aber in der Zukunft wäre es natürlich auch denkbar, intelligente Schuhsohlen bei Problemen durch Fehlbelastungen in jedem Alter zu verwenden. „Man könnte mit der Gesichtserkennung des iPhones den Fuß scannen und so eine Vorlage für eine individuelle Schuhsohle zu erhalten“, ergänzt Gabrecht. Die ersten Orthopädietechniker haben bereits Interesse. Aber bis zur finalen Anwendung ist eine kostspielige Produktentwicklung nötig.

Bund fördert Aufbau einer innovativen Forschungsinfrastruktur für Quantentechnologien, Laserphysik und Cybersicherheit in Mainfranken
Erfolgreiche Durchsetzung in der bundesweiten Förderausschreibung HAW-OpenSpace: Das hat die Technische Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS) mit ihrem Forschungsprojekt „CyberQ – Quantum Cyber Security OpenSpace“ geschafft. Das Vorhaben zählt zu insgesamt 31 Projekten, die von der Gemeinsamen Wissenschaftskonferenz (GWK) auf Grundlage einer wissenschaftlichen Begutachtung zur Förderung ausgewählt wurden. Das auf drei Jahre ausgelegte Forschungsprojekt umfasst ein beantragtes Fördervolumen von rund 1,83 Millionen Euro.
„Die Auswahl unseres Forschungsprojekts in dieser hoch dotierten Förderlinie ist ein herausragender Erfolg für die THWS“, betont Präsident Prof. Dr. Jean Meyer. „Besonders erfreulich ist, dass unsere Hochschule damit in allen neuen Förderprogrammen des Bundesministeriums für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt (BMFTR) für Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften erfolgreich vertreten ist.“ Dies unterstreiche die Forschungs- und Innovationskraft der THWS.
Interdisziplinäres Forschungsteam der THWS
Das Projekt wird von einem interdisziplinären Forschungsteam umgesetzt: Dr. Tim Koslowski, FANG sowie Quantentechnologien und Gesamtprojektleitung, Prof. Dr. Sebastian Biedermann, Cybersicherheit, und Prof. Dr. Jochen Seufert, Lasertechnologie und optische Hardwareentwicklung. Die Zusammenarbeit zwischen der Fakultät Angewandte Natur- und Geisteswissenschaften (FANG) und dem Technologietransferzentrum Cybersicherheit in Ochsenfurt (TTZ-WUE) bündelt die wissenschaftlichen und technologischen Kompetenzen der THWS. Als industrieller Anwendungspartner begleitet die nanoplus GmbH aus Gerbrunn das Forschungsvorhaben.
„CyberQ zeigt einmal mehr, welches enorme Potenzial in der interdisziplinären Zusammenarbeit an unserer Hochschule steckt“, so Prof. Dr. Jan Schmitt, Vizepräsident für Forschung und Gründung. „Durch die Verbindung unterschiedlicher wissenschaftlicher Disziplinen gelingt es uns, innovative Forschungsansätze für zentrale technologische Herausforderungen unserer Zeit zu entwickeln. Dieser Erfolg ist ein wichtiger Beitrag zur Zukunft unserer Hochschule.“
Mit CyberQ stärkt die THWS ihre Position in der Erforschung und Entwicklung zukunftsweisender Schlüsseltechnologien und schafft eine langfristig nutzbare Forschungsplattform, die auch weiteren Forschenden, Studierenden, Unternehmen und öffentlichen Einrichtungen offenstehen soll. Damit leistet das Projekt einen wichtigen Beitrag zur technologischen Souveränität Deutschlands und zur Stärkung des Innovations- und Wirtschaftsstandorts Mainfranken.
CyberQ – Sichere Kommunikation im Zeitalter der Quantencomputer
Mit CyberQ entsteht eine interdisziplinäre Forschungs- und Transferinfrastruktur für quantensichere und widerstandsfähige Kommunikationssysteme. Hintergrund ist die rasante Entwicklung von Quantencomputern, die zukünftig in der Lage sein könnten, heute weitverbreitete Verschlüsselungsverfahren zu überwinden. Insbesondere für Unternehmen, öffentliche Einrichtungen und Betreiber kritischer Infrastruktur stelle dies eine erhebliche Herausforderung dar.
CyberQ verbindet hierzu drei zukunftsweisende Forschungsgebiete: Quantentechnologien, Cybersicherheit und Laserphysik. Neben dem Einsatz quantenresistenter kryptografischer Verfahren (Post-Quanten-Kryptografie) und der quantenphysikalisch basierten Verteilung kryptografischer Schlüssel (Quantum Key Distribution, QKD) steht die Entwicklung neuartiger optischer Kommunikationssysteme im Mittelpunkt.
Ein besonderes technologisches Innovationsmerkmal ist der Aufbau einer laserbasierten Feinstrahlkommunikationsstrecke im mittleren Infrarotbereich bei einer Wellenlänge von etwa vier Mikrometern. Diese Technologie ermöglicht die drahtlose optische Datenübertragung zwischen Gebäuden und Standorten und könnte zukünftig eine wichtige Ergänzung zu bestehenden glasfaserbasierten Kommunikationsnetzen darstellen. Gleichzeitig sollen die physikalischen und technologischen Grundlagen für eine zukünftige Quantenkommunikation in diesem bislang wenig erschlossenen Wellenlängenbereich geschaffen werden. Die entwickelten Kommunikationssysteme werden unter realitätsnahen Bedingungen auf ihre Sicherheit, Leistungsfähigkeit und Widerstandsfähigkeit gegenüber Cyberangriffen und technischen Störungen untersucht.
Über die Förderinitiative
Mit der Förderinitiative HAW-OpenSpace unterstützt das BMFTR den Aufbau offener Forschungs- und Innovationsräume an Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften. Ziel ist es, die Entwicklung zentraler Schlüsseltechnologien im Rahmen der Hightech Agenda Deutschland voranzutreiben, die anwendungsorientierte Forschung zu stärken und den Technologientransfer zwischen Wissenschaft, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft zu intensivieren. Für die Fördermaßnahme stellt der Bund insgesamt rund 61 Millionen Euro zur Verfügung.
Über die THWS
Die Technische Hochschule Würzburg-Schweinfurt (THWS) zählt zu den größten Hochschulen für angewandte Wissenschaften in Bayern und steht seit ihrer Gründung im Jahr 1971 für hervorragende Lehre und angewandte Forschung. Mit rund 9.200 Studierenden, einem breit gefächerten Angebot von mehr als 60 Studiengängen sowie zwei Promotionszentren deckt die THWS ein weites Spektrum ab, das von Technik über Wirtschafts- und Sozialwissenschaften sowie Sprache bis hin zu Gestaltung reicht. Die THWS ist nicht nur regional in Franken und Bayern verwurzelt, sondern auch stark international ausgerichtet, was sich in zahlreichen Kooperationen und Austauschprogrammen weltweit und nicht zuletzt in einem vielseitigen englischsprachigen Studienangebot widerspiegelt.

Wie lassen sich in der Luftfracht Daten nahtlos vernetzen, Frachtkapazitäten mit Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI) vorausschauend planen und Transporte autonom bewegen? Antworten liefert das Forschungsprojekt »Digitales Testfeld Air Cargo« (DTAC). Seit 2021 haben Forschende des Fraunhofer-Instituts für Materialfluss und Logistik IML gemeinsam mit der Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences und neun Akteuren der Luftfrachtbranche konkrete Lösungen entwickelt. Das vom Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung (BMDS) geförderte Projekt feierte nun seinen Projektabschluss in Berlin und zeigte, wieso die Zukunft der Branche nicht in der Luft, sondern am Boden entschieden wird.
Exceltabellen, Faxen, händisches Einpflegen von Daten. Eine Zettelwirtschaft und das Transportieren von Waren hauptsächlich durch Menschen. So sieht Luftfrachtrealität bis heute aus. Eine bessere, international vernetzte Transportkette, eine digitale Prozessoptimierung und die Automatisierung der Transportwege waren die drei Hauptziele des Forschungsprojekts. Unter dem Dach von DTAC haben die Partner neue Möglichkeiten in zwei Projektphasen (1. Phase: 2021–2024, 2. Phase: 2024–2026) erarbeitet, um die Luftfrachtbranche umfassend zu verbessern.
In den fünf Jahren Forschung entstanden daraus konkrete Lösungen, die international zur Anwendung kommen: Mit NE:ONE haben die Projektbeteiligten für den internationalen Standard ONE Record der International Air Transport Association (IATA) eine Applikation entwickelt, die als Open Source der internationalen Community zur Verfügung steht und Unternehmen den Einstieg in den standardisierten Datenaustausch erleichtert. Im Teilprojekt Predictive Analytics wurden mehrere Prognosemodelle auf Basis von KI entwickelt. Eines davon sagt das Frachtaufkommen im Export und Import voraus. So können Personal, Lagerfläche und Ladehilfen optimal eingesetzt werden. Erste Auswertungen zeigen, dass die Prognosen die Planung signifikant verbessern: Auf Tagesebene liegt die Abweichung nur bei rund fünf Prozent. Im dritten Teilprojekt wurden verschiedene automatisierte und autonome Robotiksysteme für den Einsatz im Luftfrachtbereich an Flughäfen getestet und weiterentwickelt. Daraus entstanden ein verbessertes Open-Source-Leitsystem und eine neue, patentierte Multifunktionsplattform für den autonomen Transport von Luftfrachtpaletten über Hallengrenzen hinaus.
»Mit dem Projekt wird die digitale Zukunft der Luftfracht gestaltet. Hier kommen digitale Innovation und konkrete Anwendungen zusammen. Gemeinsam haben Forschung und Wirtschaft neue Zugänge geschaffen: Einstiegshürden gesenkt, Entscheidungsgrundlagen verbessert und neue Möglichkeiten für vernetzte Prozesse eröffnet. Das ›Digitale Testfeld Air Cargo‹ stärkt Deutschlands Innovationskraft und gibt der Branche wichtige Impulse, um den internationalen Wettbewerb aktiv mitzugestalten«, so Bundesdigitalminister Dr. Karsten Wildberger.
Auch international bekam das Forschungsprojekt DTAC Anerkennung: Während seiner Laufzeit wurden die Forschenden mehrfach ausgezeichnet, unter anderem mit dem »Air Cargo Sustainability Award 2025« von der International Air Cargo Association (TIACA) in Hongkong und dem »International Award for Excellence in Air Cargo 2025« von STAT Times in Nairobi. Zudem gewannen sie mehrere Luftfracht-Hackathons der IATA.
»Die Projektentwicklungen sind von entscheidender Bedeutung, um die Branche auf die Anforderungen der Zukunft vorzubereiten und die Effizienz und damit letztlich auch die Nachhaltigkeit der Luftfrachtprozesse zu verbessern«, sagte Dr. Harald Sieke, Abteilungsleiter Luftverkehrslogistik am Fraunhofer IML und Gesamtprojektleiter des DTAC, im Rahmen der Abschlussveranstaltung am 25. November in Berlin. Um den technologischen und den Wissensvorsprung weiter auszubauen, sollten laut Sieke nun alle drei Teilprojekte an realen Bedingungen getestet werden. »Jetzt wollen wir den internationalen Erfolg in die tägliche Luftfrachtpraxis übersetzen. Dafür braucht es abschließende Validierungen im realen Betrieb, um den Transfer in die breite Anwendung zu ebnen.«
Das »Digitale Testfeld Air Cargo« ist ein vom Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung (BMDS) gefördertes Forschungsprojekt mit einem Gesamtvolumen von über 18 Millionen Euro, das digitale Anwendungen für die Luftfracht entwickelte. Umgesetzt haben die Forschenden das Projekt in enger Zusammenarbeit mit der Frankfurt University of Applied Sciences (FUAS) und Konsortialpartnern aus der Luftfrachtbranche, darunter die Flughäfen Frankfurt, Köln, Leipzig und München, sowie die Industriepartner Cargogate Munich Airport, CHI Deutschland Cargo Handling, DB Schenker (heute DSV), Lufthansa Cargo und Sovereign Speed. Zudem waren CHAMP Cargosystems sowie LUG aircargo handling assoziierte Partner. Schiffspropeller sicherer auslegen: Wanddicke und Meerwasser im Fokus

Das Materialverhalten großer Schiffspropeller aus Aluminiumbronze ist entscheidend für eine sichere und werkstoffgerechte Auslegung.
| Copyright:
Fraunhofer LBF, KI-generiert mit Microsoft Copilot.
Download
Im Projekt »Bross« untersuchte das Fraunhofer-Institut für Betriebsfestigkeit und Systemzuverlässigkeit LBF mit Partnern den Einfluss von Gefüge, Wanddicke, Fertigungsbedingungen und Meerwasser. Rund 16 Prozent weniger Schwingfestigkeit zeigten Aluminiumbronze-Proben aus 400 Millimeter dicken Gussbereichen gegenüber Proben aus Bereichen mit 40 Millimeter Wanddicke. Auch Meerwasser reduziert die Schwingfestigkeit deutlich. Die Ergebnisse liefern Grundlagen für eine zuverlässigere und ressourcenschonendere Auslegung von Schiffspropellern und zeigen Potenzial für Reparaturen mittels additiver Fertigung.
Aluminiumbronze: Wie Wanddicke und Meerwasser die Schwingfestigkeit beeinflussen
Die Unterschiede in der Schwingfestigkeit zwischen den untersuchten Wanddicken gehen auf Gefügeunterschiede zurück, die bei Erstarrung und Abkühlung entstehen. Die in »Bross« untersuchten Aluminiumbronzen werden unter anderem in Schiffspropellern und Turbinen eingesetzt.
Das Fraunhofer LBF untersuchte den Einfluss von Fertigungsrandbedingungen und Korrosion auf das zyklische Werkstoffverhalten verschiedener Al-Bronze-Gusslegierungen und Wanddicken in Luft und künstlichem Meerwasser. Für die korrosiven Versuche entwickelte das Institut eigene Probengeometrien und eine Medienkammer. Die Analysen berücksichtigten auch Poren, Lunker und relevante Gefügebestandteile.
Die Untersuchungen liefern eine experimentell abgesicherte Datenbasis für die Bauteilbemessung bis in sehr hohe Schwingspielbereiche. Gegenüber den Bemessungswerten nach DNV-CG-0039 zeigt die untersuchte Standardlegierung zunächst vergleichbare, teilweise höhere Schwingfestigkeiten. Im sehr hohen Schwingspielbereich fällt die experimentell ermittelte Wöhlerlinie jedoch stärker ab.
Schiffspropeller reparieren: Potenzial der additiven Fertigung mit WAAM
Neben den Gusswerkstoffen untersuchte das Projektteam auch Werkstoffproben, die mit Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) hergestellt wurden. Unter künstlichem Meerwasser erreichten diese eine hohe Korrosionsschwingfestigkeit. Im untersuchten Bereich lag ihre Beanspruchbarkeit deutlich über der des Gusswerkstoffs. Das Verfahren ist etwa für die Reparatur beschädigter Propellerspitzen interessant. Perspektivisch könnte WAAM auch für die additive Fertigung größerer Propellerbereiche infrage kommen.
Werkstoffgerecht konstruieren und Ressourcen schonen
Gießereien, Propellerhersteller und Konstrukteure erhalten aus »Bross« Hinweise für Werkstoffauswahl, Fertigung und Bauteilauslegung. Wer Wanddicke und weitere Einflussgrößen früh berücksichtigt, kann Material bedarfsgerechter einsetzen. Dies kann Ressourcen und Energie in der Herstellung sparen. Betreiber maritimer Anlagen können zudem von langlebigeren und besser reparierbaren Komponenten profitieren.
Projektpartner und Förderung
Das Verbundprojekt »Bross« wurde von der Mecklenburger Metallguss GmbH (MMG) koordiniert. Weitere Partner waren das Fraunhofer LBF, Siemens Energy Global, Voith, Schottel, der Bundesverband der Deutschen Gießerei-Industrie (BDG) und DNV.
Das Vorhaben wurde mit Mitteln des Bundesministeriums für Wirtschaft und Klimaschutz unter dem Förderkennzeichen 03SX573B und unter Trägerschaft des Projektträgers Jülich gefördert.

Für verständliche und kontrollierbare Softwaresysteme: Sonderforschungsbereich erhält rund 13 Millionen Euro

Das Team des Sonderforschungsbereichs.

Die Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG) hat die dritte Förderperiode des Sonderforschungsbereichs/Transregio 248 „Grundlagen verständlicher Softwaresysteme – für eine nachvollziehbare cyber-physische Welt“ bewilligt. Der seit 2019 geförderte und als „Center for Perspicuous Computing“ etablierte Forschungsverbund der Universität des Saarlandes und der Technischen Universität Dresden (TUD) erhält damit eine weitere vierjährige Förderung von rund 13 Millionen Euro für seine Arbeiten an verständlichen, plausiblen und kontrollierbaren Software- und KI-Systemen.
Im Zentrum der Forschung stehen Methoden und Modelle für Software- und KI-Systeme, die ihr Verhalten, ihre Entscheidungen und die damit verbundenen Konsequenzen für den Menschen verständlich und nachvollziehbar machen. Die Bedeutung dieser Forschung nimmt angesichts der rasanten Entwicklung softwaregestützter Anwendungen mit KI-Unterstützung weiter zu: Computerprogramme übernehmen heute Aufgaben, die unmittelbar das Leben von Menschen beeinflussen, und handeln zunehmend selbständig. Autonome Fahrzeuge analysieren ihre Umgebung und treffen Entscheidungen im Straßenverkehr. Intelligente Systeme steuern industrielle Prozesse oder Kraftwerke. KI-gestützte Roboter operieren Menschen oder unterstützen die medizinische Versorgung und Pflege älterer Menschen.
Menschen müssen Entscheidungen von Maschinen verstehen können
„Wir benötigen eine Art von eingebauter Nachvollziehbarkeit, auf deren Grundlage Menschen und auch Systeme direkt handeln und eingreifen können“, erklärt Prof. Raimund Dachselt, Sprecher des Sonderforschungsbereichs. „Menschen müssen erkennen können, warum ein System zu einer Entscheidung gelangt ist, welche Konsequenzen daraus entstehen und wie sie bei Bedarf wirksam reagieren und eingreifen können.“
Damit greift der Sonderforschungsbereich/Transregio 248 auch höchstaktuelle gesellschaftliche und regulatorische Entwicklungen auf. Der EU Artificial Intelligence Act, der weltweit erste verbindliche Rechtsrahmen der Europäischen Union zur einheitlichen Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz, fordert insbesondere für Hochrisiko-Systeme wirksame menschliche Kontrolle. Diese setzt voraus, dass die relevanten Systemzustände und Entscheidungsgrundlagen zugänglich und verständlich sind – ein Kernthema des Forschungsverbundes.
Hintergrund: Sonderforschungsbereich zu verständlichen Softwaresystemen
Seit 2019 fördert die Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft das „Center for Perspicuous Computing“. Nun hat der Forschungsverbund auch die dritte und letzte Förderperiode bewilligt bekommen und erreicht damit die maximale Förderdauer von zwölf Jahren. Für die Jahre 2027 bis 2030 wurden rund 12,5 Millionen Euro beantragt.
Der Sonderforschungsbereich ist ein gemeinsames Projekt der Universität des Saarlandes und der TUD. Insgesamt vereint das „Center for Perspicuous Computing“ rund hundert Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler. Da es um Fragen geht, die weit über die Informatik hinausreichen, arbeiten im Sonderforschungsbereich interdisziplinäre Teams aus der Psychologie, Rechtswissenschaft, Philosophie und Informatik zusammen. Neben den beiden Universitäten gehören das Deutsche Forschungszentrum für Künstliche Intelligenz, das CISPA Helmholtz-Zentrum für Informationssicherheit, das Max-Planck-Institut für Softwaresysteme sowie Forschungspartner in Freiburg, Braunschweig und Wien zum Verbund. Das Team des neuen Sonderforschungsbereichs Episodic Memory
| Copyright:
SFB Episodic Memory
Download
Unser episodisches Gedächtnis – also Erinnerungen an persönlich erlebte Ereignisse – ist kein passiver Speicher. Es ist ein aktiver Konstruktionsprozess. Diese Erkenntnis wirft grundlegende Fragen auf: Wie definieren wir „konstruiert“? Warum fehlt eine einheitliche Theoriebildung? Wie wirken sich diese Lücken auf die Erforschung von Entwicklung, Traumata oder Tiergedächtnis aus? Im neuen Sonderforschungsbereich (SFB) „Episodic Memory“ gehen Forschende unter Koordination von Prof. Dr. Sen Cheng aus der Fakultät für Informatik der Ruhr-Universität Bochum diesen Fragen nach. Die Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft fördert den SFB ab 1. Januar 2027 für zunächst vier Jahre mit rund 11 Millionen Euro.
Im Zentrum des SFB steht ein innovatives Rahmenmodell: Das Gehirn konstruiert ein Szenario, wenn es Informationen aus der Vergangenheit abruft. Es kombiniert episodische Gedächtnisspuren mit semantischem Wissen, passt sie flexibel an Kontexte an, etwa soziale Situationen oder das Selbstbild, und füllt Lücken auf. Der Forschungsverbund identifiziert sieben zentrale Themen, die von neuronalen Grundlagen bis zu sozialen Funktionen reichen.
Mittels modernster Methoden – von Verhaltensstudien über Bildgebung bis zu klinischen Langzeitstudien – werden die Forschenden Hypothesen testen, die sowohl philosophische Theorien als auch computergestützte Modelle voranbringen. Ziel ist es, das Verständnis des episodischen Gedächtnisses grundlegend zu erweitern und damit die Basis für zukünftige Therapien bei Gedächtnisstörungen zu legen.
Kooperationspartner
Neben Forschenden der Ruhr-Universität Bochum sind an dem Sonderforschungsbereich Gruppen der Technischen Universität Dortmund, der Universität Münster, der Technischen Hochschule Köln, der Goethe-Universität Frankfurt sowie der Universität Göttingen beteiligt.
